Attack description

An attacker compels a non-restricted mobile application to execute arbitrary code or code files through Hooking, aiming to bypass Root/Jailbreak detection. Users of mobile devices frequently Root/Jailbreak their devices to obtain administrative access to the mobile operating system and/or to install third-party mobile applications that are not available through authorized application stores (such as Google Play Store and Apple App Store). Attackers may additionally utilize these abilities to elevate their privileges or to circumvent access control on legitimate applications. Although numerous mobile applications perform checks to determine if a device is Rooted/Jailbroken before permitting authorized use of the application, attackers may manage to "hook" code to evade these checks. Successfully bypassing Root/Jailbreak detection enables an attacker to run administrative commands, access sensitive data, impersonate legitimate application users, and more.

Attack description

An adversary can exploit a flaw in Bluetooth key negotiation allowing them to decrypt information sent between two devices communicating via Bluetooth. The adversary uses an Adversary in the Middle setup to modify packets sent between the two devices during the authentication process, specifically the entropy bits. Knowledge of the number of entropy bits will allow the attacker to easily decrypt information passing over the line of communication.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Adversaries might seek to insert themselves between two or more networked devices using the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique, facilitating subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By exploiting characteristics of standard networking protocols that dictate the flow of network traffic (e.g., ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries can compel a device to route communications through a system they control, allowing them to gather information or undertake further activities. (Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For instance, adversaries might alter the DNS settings of a victim to facilitate other nefarious actions, such as blocking or redirecting users from legitimate websites and/or deploying additional malware. (Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Furthermore, adversaries can manipulate DNS and exploit their intermediary position to capture user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)). (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) Additionally, [Downgrade Attacks](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689) may be employed to attain an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, outdated, or weaker version of a communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm. (Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Adversaries may also use their AiTM position to monitor and/or alter traffic, as seen in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). They can establish a setup akin to AiTM to obstruct traffic from reaching its intended destination, which may serve to weaken defenses and/or assist in executing a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

Attack description

An attacker takes advantage of a flaw in how an application locates external libraries to manipulate the flow of execution, redirecting it to a library or code base provided by the attacker. This type of attack enables the attacker to compromise either the application or the server by executing unauthorized code. Typically, an application makes function calls that are part of libraries that exist outside of the application itself. These libraries might be integral components of the operating system or could be third-party libraries. If an attacker manages to reroute the application’s requests for these libraries to alternative libraries that the attacker controls, they can compel the targeted application to run arbitrary code. This scenario is particularly hazardous when the targeted application possesses elevated privileges. Access redirection can be achieved through various techniques, such as symbolic links, modification of the search path, and manipulation of relative paths.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Network Service Discovery Threat actors may seek to compile a list of services that are operational on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, particularly those that could be susceptible to remote software exploitation. To gather this information, common approaches include conducting port, vulnerability, and/or wordlist scans by employing tools that are introduced onto a system. (Citation: CISA AR21-126A FIVEHANDS May 2021) In cloud environments, adversaries may endeavor to uncover services that are active on other cloud hosts. Furthermore, if the cloud setup is linked to an on-premises environment, adversaries might also pinpoint services that are functioning on non-cloud systems. In macOS environments, adversaries may leverage the built-in Bonjour application to identify services operating on other macOS hosts within the same network. The mDNSResponder daemon associated with Bonjour automatically registers and promotes the services that a host has registered on the network. For instance, adversaries can initiate an mDNS query (for example, dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp .) to locate other systems that are broadcasting the ssh service. (Citation: apple doco bonjour description)(Citation: macOS APT Activity Bradley)

Necessary resources

The attacker needs either a network mapping or scanning tool, or they must perform socket programming via the command line. Packet injection tools can also be beneficial for this task. Depending on the approach taken, it may be essential to sniff the network to observe the response.

Adversary Context in ATT&CK

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Attackers can manipulate Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to insert themselves between the communications of multiple networked devices. This tactic can facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol serves the purpose of converting IPv4 addresses into link layer addresses, including media access control (MAC) addresses. Devices within a local network segment interact with one another using these link layer addresses. In instances where a networked device lacks the link layer address of another device, it may issue a broadcast ARP request within the local network to resolve the corresponding IP address to a MAC address. The device corresponding to the specified IP address responds directly with its MAC address. Subsequently, the networked device that initiated the ARP request will utilize and store this information in its ARP cache.

An attacker may passively monitor for an ARP request to corrupt the ARP cache of the device that made the request. By responding with their own MAC address, the attacker misleads the victim into thinking they are communicating with the intended device. For successful ARP cache poisoning, the attacker’s reply must be faster than that of the legitimate owner of the IP address. Additionally, attackers can issue a gratuitous ARP reply that falsely claims ownership of a specific IP address to all devices in the local network segment.

Since the ARP protocol is stateless and does not implement authentication, devices may inadvertently add or update the MAC address associated with an IP address in their ARP cache. 

Attackers might exploit ARP cache poisoning to intercept network traffic. This method can be employed to gather and/or relay sensitive information such as credentials, particularly those transmitted over insecure, unencrypted protocols.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Thread Execution Hijacking Adversaries can introduce malicious code into compromised processes to bypass process-based defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges. Thread Execution Hijacking refers to the technique of running arbitrary code within the address space of an active, separate process. This method typically involves suspending a target process, followed by unmapping or hollowing out its memory, which then allows for the insertion of malicious code or the specification of a DLL path. Initially, a handle to the targeted victim process is generated using native Windows API functions such as OpenThread. Subsequently, the process can be suspended, modified to align with the injected code, and then resumed through a sequence of commands: SuspendThread , VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, and finally ResumeThread (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017). This technique closely resembles [Process Hollowing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012) but focuses on manipulating an existing process instead of generating a new process in a suspended state. Executing code within the context of another process could grant access to that process's memory, system or network resources, and may also offer elevated privileges. Additionally, execution through Thread Execution Hijacking might circumvent detection by security products as the execution appears to be concealed under a legitimate process.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Exploit Public-Facing Application

Adversaries might seek to take advantage of a vulnerability in a host or system that is accessible over the Internet as a means to gain initial entry into a network. The vulnerability present in the system could stem from a software flaw, a transient issue, or a misconfiguration.

The applications that are exploited frequently consist of websites or web servers, but they can also encompass databases (such as SQL), common services (like SMB or SSH), management and administration protocols for network devices (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other systems with open sockets that are reachable via the Internet. (Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) In the context of ESXi infrastructure, adversaries might target exposed OpenSLP services or exploit VMware vCenter servers that are accessible. (Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the type of vulnerability that is being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

When applications are hosted on cloud infrastructure and/or utilize containerization, exploiting them can result in the compromise of the underlying instance or container. This may provide adversaries with a means to access cloud or container APIs (for instance, through the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit access to the container host via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or leverage inadequate identity and access management practices.

Adversaries might also target edge network infrastructure and associated appliances, specifically focusing on devices that lack strong host-based security measures. (Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 list the most prevalent vulnerabilities associated with the web. (Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)

**Technique:** Password Spraying

Adversaries might employ a singular or a limited selection of frequently used passwords against numerous accounts in an effort to obtain valid account credentials. This technique involves utilizing one password (for instance, 'Password01') or a concise list of widely accepted passwords that align with the domain's complexity requirements. By attempting logins with that password across various accounts on a network, they aim to sidestep account lockouts that typically arise when attempting to brute force a single account with multiple passwords. (Citation: BlackHillsInfosec Password Spraying)

Password spraying generally targets management services over frequently used ports. The services that are commonly the focus of these attacks include:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

Besides management services, adversaries may also "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications that utilize federated authentication protocols," including externally accessible email applications like Office 365. (Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)

To evade detection thresholds, adversaries might intentionally limit their password spraying attempts to prevent activating security alerts. Furthermore, they may take advantage of LDAP and Kerberos authentication attempts, which are less likely to provoke noticeable events such as Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625, commonly triggered by unsuccessful SMB connection attempts. (Citation: Microsoft Storm-0940)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Impair Command History Logging Adversaries may impair command history logging to hide commands they run on a compromised system. Various command interpreters keep track of the commands users type in their terminal so that users can retrace what they've done. On Linux and macOS, command history is tracked in a file pointed to by the environment variable HISTFILE. When a user logs off a system, this information is flushed to a file in the user's home directory called ~/.bash_history. The HISTCONTROL environment variable keeps track of what should be saved by the history command and eventually into the ~/.bash_history file when a user logs out. HISTCONTROL does not exist by default on macOS, but can be set by the user and will be respected. The `HISTFILE` environment variable is also used in some ESXi systems.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) Adversaries may clear the history environment variable (unset HISTFILE) or set the command history size to zero (export HISTFILESIZE=0) to prevent logging of commands. Additionally, HISTCONTROL can be configured to ignore commands that start with a space by simply setting it to "ignorespace". HISTCONTROL can also be set to ignore duplicate commands by setting it to "ignoredups". In some Linux systems, this is set by default to "ignoreboth" which covers both of the previous examples. This means that “ ls” will not be saved, but “ls” would be saved by history. Adversaries can abuse this to operate without leaving traces by simply prepending a space to all of their terminal commands. On Windows systems, the PSReadLine module tracks commands used in all PowerShell sessions and writes them to a file ($env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt by default). Adversaries may change where these logs are saved using Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySavePath {File Path}. This will cause ConsoleHost_history.txt to stop receiving logs. Additionally, it is possible to turn off logging to this file using the PowerShell command Set-PSReadlineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing.(Citation: Microsoft PowerShell Command History)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell command audit)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell Command History Forensics) Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to disable historical command logging (e.g. no logging).

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Space after Filename Adversaries are capable of concealing a program's actual file type by altering the extension of a file. For specific file types (notably, this does not apply to .app extensions), adding a space at the end of a filename will influence how the operating system processes the file. For instance, if there exists a Mach-O executable file named evil.bin, a user double-clicking it will result in Terminal.app launching and executing the file. Conversely, if this file is renamed to evil.txt, double-clicking it will open it with the default text editing application (thereby preventing the binary from executing). However, should the file be renamed to evil.txt (with a space at the end), upon double-clicking by a user, the operating system will correctly identify the true file type and handle it accordingly, leading to the execution of the binary (Citation: Mac Backdoors are back). Adversaries can exploit this capability to deceive users into double-clicking files that appear harmless, irrespective of their format, ultimately resulting in the execution of malicious content.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Terminal Services DLL Adversaries can exploit elements of Terminal Services to facilitate persistent access to systems. Microsoft Terminal Services, which was renamed Remote Desktop Services in certain Windows Server operating systems starting in 2022, allows for remote terminal connections to hosts. Terminal Services provides the capability for servers to deliver a complete, interactive graphical user interface to clients through RDP. (Citation: Microsoft Remote Desktop Services) [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003)s operating as a "generic" process (for example, svchost.exe) load the service's DLL file, with the location recorded in a Registry entry known as ServiceDll. (Citation: Microsoft System Services Fundamentals) The termsrv.dll file, usually found in `%SystemRoot%\System32\`, is the standard ServiceDll value for Terminal Services located at `HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\services\TermService\Parameters\`. Adversaries might alter and/or substitute the Terminal Services DLL to gain persistent access to compromised hosts. (Citation: James TermServ DLL) Changes made to this DLL can be intended to execute arbitrary payloads (while also potentially maintaining the regular functionality of termsrv.dll) as well as to enable exploitable features of Terminal Services. **Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to create a denial of service (DoS) by overwhelming a target with a significant amount of network traffic. This type of DoS attack can lead to diminished availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) techniques involve utilizing one or more systems to direct a high volume of network packets towards the network of the targeted service. A wide range of network protocols can be employed for flooding purposes. While stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently utilized, stateful protocols such as TCP can also be leveraged.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are often executed using botnets. Large botnets can produce a considerable amount of traffic originating from systems distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries might either possess the means to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or opt to lease time on an already existing botnet to perform their attacks. In severe cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), an extensive number of systems may be enlisted to create the flood, allowing each to transmit only a minimal amount of traffic while still achieving sufficient volume to saturate the target network. Under these conditions, differentiating DDoS traffic from legitimate users becomes extremely challenging. Some of the most notable DDoS flooding incidents, including the 2012 series of attacks aimed at prominent US banks, have involved botnets. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

By inserting an entry into the "run keys" within the Registry or startup folder, the corresponding program will be triggered to run when a user logs in. (Citation: Microsoft Run Key) These programs will be executed in the context of the user, inheriting the associated permissions of the account. Windows systems by default create the following run keys: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Run keys may be present across multiple hives. (Citation: Microsoft Wow6432Node 2018)(Citation: Malwarebytes Wow6432Node 2016) The HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx key is also available but is not automatically created in Windows Vista and subsequent versions. Entries in the Registry run key can directly reference programs or specify them as dependencies. (Citation: Microsoft Run Key) For instance, a DLL can be loaded at user logon by employing a "Depend" key with RunOnceEx: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil[.]dll" (Citation: Oddvar Moe RunOnceEx Mar 2018) Adding a program to a startup folder will similarly trigger its execution upon user login. There exists a startup folder for individual user accounts as well as a universal startup folder that will be checked irrespective of the user account that logs in. The path to the startup folder for the current user can be found at C:\Users\\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, while the path for all users is located at C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp. **Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to achieve a denial of service (DoS) by inundating a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This type of DoS attack can compromise both the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or more systems direct a high volume of network packets toward the network of the targeted service. Almost any network protocol can be exploited for flooding, with stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP being frequently utilized, though stateful protocols such as TCP can also be employed.

Network flooding attacks against networks and services are often carried out using botnets. Extensive botnets can produce considerable traffic from systems dispersed across the global Internet. Adversaries may either possess the capacity to construct and maintain their own botnet infrastructure or may choose to lease time on an existing botnet for executing an attack. In severe instances of distributed DoS (DDoS), the number of systems involved in generating the flood can be so high that each system is only required to send a minimal amount of traffic, which collectively suffices to overwhelm the target network. Under these conditions, it becomes extremely challenging to differentiate DDoS traffic from that of legitimate clients. Some of the most notorious DDoS flooding attacks have utilized botnets, including the series of incidents in 2012 that targeted major banks in the United States. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order used to load other programs. Because some programs do not call other programs using the full path, adversaries may place their own file in the directory where the calling program is located, causing the operating system to launch their malicious software at the request of the calling program. Search order hijacking occurs when an adversary abuses the order in which Windows searches for programs that are not given a path. Unlike [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001) search order hijacking, the search order differs depending on the method that is used to execute the program. (Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess) (Citation: Windows NT Command Shell) (Citation: Microsoft WinExec) However, it is common for Windows to search in the directory of the initiating program before searching through the Windows system directory. An adversary who finds a program vulnerable to search order hijacking (i.e., a program that does not specify the path to an executable) may take advantage of this vulnerability by creating a program named after the improperly specified program and placing it within the initiating program's directory. For example, "example.exe" runs "cmd.exe" with the command-line argument net user. An adversary may place a program called "net.exe" within the same directory as example.exe, "net.exe" will be run instead of the Windows system utility net. In addition, if an adversary places a program called "net.com" in the same directory as "net.exe", then cmd.exe /C net user will execute "net.com" instead of "net.exe" due to the order of executable extensions defined under PATHEXT. (Citation: Microsoft Environment Property) Search order hijacking is also a common practice for hijacking DLL loads and is covered in [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001).

**Technique:** Process Injection

Adversaries can inject code into existing processes to bypass defenses that are based on process monitoring and potentially gain higher privileges. Process injection is a technique that allows arbitrary code to be executed within the address space of another active process. By running code within the context of a different process, adversaries may gain access to that process's memory, as well as system and network resources, and may even achieve elevated permissions. Additionally, executing code through process injection can help avoid detection by security solutions, as the activity is concealed within a legitimate process.

There are various methods to inject code into a process, many of which exploit legitimate features. These techniques are available across all major operating systems but are generally specific to each platform.

More advanced examples may carry out multiple process injections to partition modules and further reduce the likelihood of detection, utilizing named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) methods as a means of communication.

**Technique:** Credential Stuffing

Adversaries often leverage credentials extracted from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to infiltrate target accounts via credential overlap. Large quantities of username and password combinations can sometimes be found online following the compromise of a website or service, where user account credentials are accessed. This data can be advantageous for adversaries seeking to breach accounts, capitalizing on the common behavior of users who tend to reuse passwords across both personal and professional accounts.

Credential stuffing poses significant risks, as it may lead to a high volume of authentication failures and subsequent account lockouts, contingent upon the organization's policies regarding login failures.

When performing credential stuffing, attackers typically utilize management services that operate over frequently used ports. The following services are commonly targeted:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

Beyond management services, adversaries may also focus on "single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications that utilize federated authentication protocols," in addition to externally accessible email applications like Office 365. (Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Path Interception via Search Order Hijacking Adversaries can deploy their malicious payloads by manipulating the search order utilized for loading other programs. Since certain programs do not invoke other programs with a complete path, adversaries can introduce their own files into the directory of the calling program, leading the operating system to execute their malicious software upon the calling program's request. Search order hijacking takes place when an adversary exploits the sequence in which Windows looks for programs that lack a specified path. Unlike [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001) search order hijacking, the search sequence varies based on the execution method of the program. (Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess) (Citation: Windows NT Command Shell) (Citation: Microsoft WinExec) Nevertheless, it is typical for Windows to first search in the directory of the initiating program before checking the Windows system directory. An adversary who discovers a program susceptible to search order hijacking (i.e., one that fails to specify the path to an executable) can exploit this flaw by creating a program that shares the name of the incorrectly specified program and placing it in the initiating program's directory. For instance, if "example.exe" executes "cmd.exe" with the command-line argument net user, an adversary might place a program named "net.exe" in the same directory as example.exe. Consequently, "net.exe" would be executed in place of the Windows system utility net. Furthermore, if an adversary also places a program called "net.com" in the same directory as "net.exe," then cmd.exe /C net user will run "net.com" rather than "net.exe" due to the order of executable extensions as determined by PATHEXT. (Citation: Microsoft Environment Property) Search order hijacking is frequently employed for hijacking DLL loads, and this technique is discussed in [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001).

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Steal Web Session Cookie

An adversary could capture session cookies from web applications or services and utilize them to access these web applications or Internet services as an authenticated user without requiring credentials. Typically, web applications and services employ session cookies as authentication tokens once a user has logged into a website.

Cookies frequently remain valid for an extended duration, even if the web application is not in active use. These cookies can be located on disk, within the browser's process memory, and in network traffic directed towards remote systems. Furthermore, other applications running on the target machine may keep sensitive authentication cookies in memory (for example, applications that authenticate with cloud services). Session cookies can also facilitate the circumvention of certain multi-factor authentication protocols. (Citation: Pass The Cookie)

Numerous malware examples specifically target cookies from web browsers on the local machine. (Citation: Kaspersky TajMahal April 2019)(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019) Adversaries might also acquire cookies by injecting harmful JavaScript code into websites or by employing [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) to deceive victims into executing malicious JavaScript in their browsers. (Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)

Additionally, there are open-source frameworks like `Evilginx2` and `Muraena` that can collect session cookies through a malicious proxy (e.g., [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557)), which can be established by an adversary and deployed in phishing attacks. (Citation: Github evilginx2)(Citation: GitHub Mauraena)

Once an adversary obtains a valid cookie, they can utilize the [Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004) technique to log in to the relevant web application.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Network Sniffing

Adversaries may engage in passive network traffic sniffing to gather information about an environment, including any authentication materials transmitted across the network. Network sniffing involves utilizing the network interface of a system to observe or collect information conveyed over either wired or wireless connections. An adversary might configure a network interface to operate in promiscuous mode, thereby passively accessing data that is currently in transit, or they could employ span ports to capture a larger volume of data.

Data obtained through this technique could encompass user credentials, particularly those transmitted via insecure, unencrypted protocols. Methods for name service resolution poisoning, such as [Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001), can also facilitate the capture of credentials for websites, proxies, and internal systems by rerouting traffic towards the adversary.

Network sniffing has the potential to disclose configuration information, including active services, version numbers, and other network details (e.g., IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) that are essential for subsequent [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) operations. It is likely that adversaries will also employ network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to passively acquire further insights into the environment.

In cloud environments, adversaries can still utilize traffic mirroring services to sniff network traffic from virtual machines. For instance, services such as AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap enable users to specify particular instances for traffic collection and designated targets for sending the collected traffic. (Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) A significant portion of this traffic may be transmitted in cleartext due to the implementation of TLS termination at the load balancer level, which alleviates the burden of encrypting and decrypting traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) The adversary might then employ exfiltration techniques such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account to access the sniffed traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries may execute network captures utilizing [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands like `monitor capture`. (Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries might seek to achieve a denial of service (DoS) by inundating a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This DoS attack can impair the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or multiple systems direct a high volume of network packets at the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be employed for flooding; however, stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are often utilized, while stateful protocols such as TCP can also be applied.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are frequently executed using botnets. Large-scale botnets have the capability to create a considerable amount of traffic from systems distributed across the globe. Adversaries may either develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or lease time on an existing botnet to carry out an attack. In severe cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), an extensive number of systems may contribute to the flood, requiring each to transmit only a minimal amount of traffic to generate enough volume to overwhelm the target network. In these situations, it becomes increasingly challenging to differentiate DDoS traffic from that of legitimate clients. Some of the most notable DDoS flooding attacks, including the series of incidents in 2012 targeting major US banks, have utilized botnets. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

Attack description

By exploiting the manner in which service accounts utilize Kerberos authentication alongside Service Principal Names (SPNs), the attacker gains access to and subsequently cracks the hashed credentials of a targeted service account in order to leverage its privileges. The Kerberos authentication protocol is founded on a ticketing system that facilitates the request and granting of access to services, as well as the ability to access those services. Once the adversary is authenticated, they can request Active Directory and acquire a service ticket, where portions are encrypted using RC4 with the private key of the authenticated account. By extracting the local ticket and storing it on disk, the attacker can perform a brute-force attack on the hashed value to uncover the credentials of the target account.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Kerberoasting

Adversaries may abuse a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or sniff network traffic to obtain a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that may be vulnerable to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110).(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) 

Service principal names (SPNs) are used to uniquely identify each instance of a Windows service. To enable authentication, Kerberos requires that SPNs be associated with at least one service logon account (an account specifically tasked with running a service(Citation: Microsoft Detecting Kerberoasting Feb 2018)).(Citation: Microsoft SPN)(Citation: Microsoft SetSPN)(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)(Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

Adversaries possessing a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) may request one or more Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) service tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC).(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) Portions of these tickets may be encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, meaning the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the service account associated with the SPN is used as the private key and is thus vulnerable to offline [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) attacks that may expose plaintext credentials.(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016) (Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

This same behavior could be executed using service tickets captured from network traffic.(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)

**Technique:** Valid Accounts

Adversaries may acquire and exploit the credentials of legitimate accounts to achieve Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Compromised credentials can facilitate bypassing access controls imposed on various resources within network systems and may also be utilized for sustained access to remote systems and externally accessible services, such as VPNs, Outlook Web Access, network devices, and remote desktop. (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW) These credentials can provide adversaries with elevated privileges to specific systems or enable entry to restricted sections of the network. Instead of deploying malware or tools alongside the legitimate access afforded by these credentials, adversaries may opt to rely solely on them to reduce the likelihood of detection.

In certain instances, adversaries might exploit dormant accounts, such as those associated with individuals who have left an organization. Utilizing these accounts can help adversaries avoid detection since the original account holder is not available to notice any unusual activity occurring on their account. (Citation: CISA MFA PrintNightmare)

The shared permissions between local, domain, and cloud accounts across a network of systems raise concerns, as adversaries may navigate across accounts and systems to attain a high level of access (e.g., domain or enterprise administrator) and circumvent access controls established within the enterprise. (Citation: TechNet Credential Theft)

**Technique:** Credential Stuffing

Adversaries might leverage credentials acquired from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to access target accounts via credential overlap. Occasionally, vast quantities of username and password combinations are exposed online when a service or website is breached and the user account credentials are retrieved. This information can be advantageous for an adversary seeking to compromise accounts, capitalizing on users' propensity to reuse the same passwords across both personal and business accounts.

Credential stuffing poses a considerable risk as it may lead to multiple authentication failures and account lockouts, contingent on the organization's policies regarding login failures.

Typically, management services operating over frequently used ports are employed when executing credential stuffing. Commonly targeted services include:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

Alongside management services, adversaries may also focus on "single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications using federated authentication protocols," in addition to externally accessible email applications like Office 365. (Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Services Registry Permissions Weakness Adversaries can deploy their malicious payloads by taking control of the Registry entries associated with services. Vulnerabilities in the permissions assigned to Registry keys that pertain to services may enable adversaries to redirect the originally designated executable to one that they control, thereby executing their code when a service is initiated. Windows retains local service configuration data in the Registry at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. The data associated with a service's Registry keys can be altered to adjust a service's execution parameters using utilities such as the service controller, sc.exe, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001), or [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075). Access to Registry keys is governed by access control lists and user permissions. (Citation: Registry Key Security)(Citation: malware_hides_service) If user and group permissions are incorrectly configured, granting access to the Registry keys for a service, adversaries may modify the service's binPath/ImagePath to direct it to a different executable that they control. When the service is initiated or restarted, the adversary-controlled application will run, enabling the adversary to achieve persistence and/or escalate privileges to the account context under which the service operates (local/domain account, SYSTEM, LocalService, or NetworkService). Adversaries may also manipulate additional Registry keys within the service’s Registry hierarchy. For instance, the FailureCommand key could be modified so that the service executes in an elevated context whenever it fails or is deliberately corrupted. (Citation: Kansa Service related collectors)(Citation: Tweet Registry Perms Weakness) The Performance key holds the name of a driver service's performance DLL along with the names of various exported functions within that DLL. (Citation: microsoft_services_registry_tree) If the Performance key is absent and an adversary-controlled user possesses the Create Subkey privilege, adversaries may create the Performance key within the service’s Registry tree to point to a malicious DLL. (Citation: insecure_reg_perms) Additionally, adversaries may introduce the Parameters key, which can reference file paths for malicious drivers. This technique has been recognized as a means of exploitation through the configuration of DLL file paths within the Parameters key of a particular service's registry setup. By inserting and configuring the Parameters key to point to a malicious DLL, adversaries can guarantee that their code is persistently loaded whenever the corresponding service or library is called. For example, the registry path (Citation: MDSec) HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WinSock2\Parameters (Citation: hexacorn)(Citation: gendigital) includes the AutodiaDLL value, which indicates the DLL to be utilized for autodial functionality. An adversary could adjust the AutodiaDLL to reference a hijacked or malicious DLL: "AutodialDLL"="c:\temp\foo.dll" This ensures persistence, as it compels the DLL (in this case, foo.dll) to be loaded each time the Winsock 2 library is accessed.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Pass the Hash

Adversaries may “pass the hash” using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the hash (PtH) is a method of authenticating as a user without having access to the user's cleartext password. This method bypasses standard authentication steps that require a cleartext password, moving directly into the portion of the authentication that uses the password hash.

When performing PtH, valid password hashes for the account being used are captured using a [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) technique. Captured hashes are used with PtH to authenticate as that user. Once authenticated, PtH may be used to perform actions on local or remote systems.

Adversaries may also use stolen password hashes to "overpass the hash." Similar to PtH, this involves using a password hash to authenticate as a user but also uses the password hash to create a valid Kerberos ticket. This ticket can then be used to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks.(Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash)

Attack description

An adversary exploits a vulnerability in an application that fails to verify the integrity of the active process, enabling the execution of arbitrary code within the address space of another active process. By utilizing executable code within the context of a different process, the adversary may attempt to access that process's memory, as well as system and network resources. The objective of this attack is to circumvent detection mechanisms and elevate privileges by concealing malicious code within a legitimate existing process. Various methods may be employed, including but not limited to: dynamic-link library (DLL) injection, portable executable injection, thread execution hijacking, ptrace system calls, VDSO hijacking, function hooking, reflective code loading, and additional techniques.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Adversaries might try to insert themselves between two or more devices on a network by employing the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique. This strategy can facilitate follow-on activities such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By taking advantage of vulnerabilities in standard networking protocols that dictate the direction of network traffic (e.g., ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries can coerce a device into routing communications through a system under their control, allowing them to gather data or execute further actions. (Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For instance, attackers might alter the DNS settings of a victim to facilitate other malicious operations, including redirecting users away from legitimate websites and/or delivering additional malware. (Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Additionally, adversaries can manipulate DNS and use their intermediary role to capture user credentials, which may include access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)). (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689) tactics may also be employed to achieve an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, outdated, or inferior version of a communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption method. (Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Moreover, adversaries could exploit their AiTM position to monitor or alter traffic, as seen in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). They can establish a setup akin to AiTM to obstruct traffic from reaching its intended destination, potentially undermining defenses or facilitating a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to initiate a denial of service (DoS) by directly transmitting a significant volume of network traffic to a specific target. This form of DoS attack can diminish both the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) refers to scenarios where one or multiple systems are employed to direct a high volume of network packets at the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be exploited for flooding purposes. Stateless protocols, such as UDP or ICMP, are frequently utilized; however, stateful protocols like TCP can also be employed.

Botnets are often leveraged to execute network flooding assaults against various networks and services. Large-scale botnets have the capacity to produce substantial traffic from systems distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries may possess the means to establish and manage their own botnet infrastructure or may opt to rent resources on an existing botnet for their attack. In some of the most severe instances of distributed DoS (DDoS), an extensive number of systems are deployed to create the flood, allowing each one to transmit only a minimal amount of traffic, sufficient to overwhelm the target network. Under these conditions, it becomes highly challenging to differentiate DDoS traffic from that of legitimate clients. Botnets have been instrumental in some of the most notable DDoS flooding incidents, including the series of attacks in 2012 that aimed at prominent US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

Adversaries might exploit a legitimate Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or monitor network traffic to acquire a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that can be susceptible to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110). Service principal names (SPNs) serve to uniquely designate each occurrence of a Windows service. For authentication to occur, Kerberos necessitates that SPNs be linked to at least one service logon account, which is specifically designated for operating a service (Citation: Microsoft Detecting Kerberoasting Feb 2018). (Citation: Microsoft SPN) (Citation: Microsoft SetSPN) (Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014) (Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Password Spraying

Adversaries might employ a singular password or a limited selection of frequently used passwords against numerous accounts in an effort to gain valid account credentials. The technique of password spraying involves utilizing one specific password (e.g., 'Password01') or a concise list of commonly adopted passwords that could comply with the domain's complexity requirements. Attempts to log in with that password are made across a variety of accounts on a network to circumvent account lockouts that typically happen when brute-force methods target a single account with multiple passwords. (Citation: BlackHillsInfosec Password Spraying)

Generally, management services that operate over well-known ports are utilized during password spraying. The services that are most frequently targeted include:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

Alongside management services, adversaries may also focus on single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications that utilize federated authentication protocols, as well as externally accessible email platforms like Office 365. (Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)

To evade detection thresholds, adversaries might intentionally slow down their password spraying attempts to prevent triggering security alerts. Moreover, they may exploit LDAP and Kerberos authentication attempts, which are less likely to provoke high-visibility alerts, such as the Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625 commonly associated with unsuccessful SMB connection tries. (Citation: Microsoft Storm-0940)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Service Exhaustion Flood

Adversaries may target the different network services provided by systems to conduct a denial of service (DoS). Adversaries often target the availability of DNS and web services, however others have been targeted as well.(Citation: Arbor AnnualDoSreport Jan 2018) Web server software can be attacked through a variety of means, some of which apply generally while others are specific to the software being used to provide the service.

One example of this type of attack is known as a simple HTTP flood, where an adversary sends a large number of HTTP requests to a web server to overwhelm it and/or an application that runs on top of it. This flood relies on raw volume to accomplish the objective, exhausting any of the various resources required by the victim software to provide the service.(Citation: Cloudflare HTTPflood)

Another variation, known as a SSL renegotiation attack, takes advantage of a protocol feature in SSL/TLS. The SSL/TLS protocol suite includes mechanisms for the client and server to agree on an encryption algorithm to use for subsequent secure connections. If SSL renegotiation is enabled, a request can be made for renegotiation of the crypto algorithm. In a renegotiation attack, the adversary establishes a SSL/TLS connection and then proceeds to make a series of renegotiation requests. Because the cryptographic renegotiation has a meaningful cost in computation cycles, this can cause an impact to the availability of the service when done in volume.(Citation: Arbor SSLDoS April 2012)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Services Registry Permissions Weakness Adversaries can launch their own malicious payloads by taking control of the Registry entries associated with services. Vulnerabilities in the permissions assigned to Registry keys linked to services may permit adversaries to reroute the originally designated executable to one they possess, thereby executing their code when the service initiates. Windows retains local service configuration data in the Registry at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. The data found within a service's Registry keys can be altered to change the execution parameters of a service using tools such as the service controller, sc.exe, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001), or [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075). Access to Registry keys is regulated through access control lists and user permissions. (Citation: Registry Key Security)(Citation: malware_hides_service) If the permissions for users and groups are not configured correctly, granting access to the Registry keys associated with a service, adversaries may modify the service's binPath/ImagePath to redirect to an executable under their control. When the service starts or is rebooted, the adversary-controlled application will run, enabling the adversary to achieve persistence and/or privilege escalation to the account context under which the service operates (local/domain account, SYSTEM, LocalService, or NetworkService). Adversaries may also manipulate additional Registry keys within the service’s Registry structure. For instance, the FailureCommand key could be altered so that the service runs in an elevated context every time it fails or is deliberately compromised. (Citation: Kansa Service related collectors)(Citation: Tweet Registry Perms Weakness) The Performance key holds the name of a driver service's performance DLL along with the names of several functions exported by the DLL. (Citation: microsoft_services_registry_tree) If the Performance key does not already exist and if a user controlled by the adversary has the Create Subkey permission, adversaries can create the Performance key within the service’s Registry tree to target a malicious DLL. (Citation: insecure_reg_perms) Additionally, adversaries may introduce the Parameters key, which can point to the file paths of malicious drivers. This technique has been recognized as a method of exploitation by setting DLL file paths within the Parameters key of a service's registry configuration. By configuring the Parameters key to reference a malicious DLL, adversaries can ensure their code is persistently loaded whenever the corresponding service or library is referenced. ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Adversaries can compromise Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to insert themselves into the communication path between two or more devices on a network. This tactic may facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol serves the purpose of converting IPv4 addresses into link layer addresses, specifically media access control (MAC) addresses. Devices within the same local network segment communicate by utilizing link layer addresses. When a device does not possess the link layer address for another device, it may issue a broadcast ARP request over the local network to resolve an IP address into a MAC address. The device that has the specified IP address responds directly with its MAC address. The device that initiated the ARP request then utilizes and saves this information in its ARP cache.

An adversary might passively observe for an ARP request to contaminate the ARP cache of the requesting device. By responding with their own MAC address, the adversary misleads the victim into believing they are interacting with the intended networked device. To successfully poison the ARP cache, the adversary’s reply must occur more swiftly than that of the legitimate owner of the IP address. Additionally, adversaries can issue a gratuitous ARP reply that falsely claims ownership of a specific IP address to all devices within the local network segment.

Since the ARP protocol is stateless and lacks authentication, devices can mistakenly add or modify the MAC address associated with an IP address in their ARP cache.

Adversaries may leverage ARP cache poisoning as a strategy to capture network traffic. This activity can be employed to gather and/or transmit sensitive information such as credentials, particularly those transmitted over insecure, unencrypted protocols.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Embedded Payloads

Adversaries can conceal malicious content by embedding payloads within other files, thereby evading detection by defenses. Files that appear to be harmless, such as executables and scripts, may be exploited to transport and obscure these malicious payloads. In certain instances, these embedded payloads can also allow adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) by not interfering with execution controls like digital signatures and notarization tickets. (Citation: Sentinel Labs)

Payloads may be embedded by adversaries in a variety of file formats to obscure their presence. (Citation: Microsoft Learn) This technique is akin to [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), although it does not necessitate the incorporation of malicious content into specific byte sequences and patterns that correspond with legitimate digital media formats. (Citation: GitHub PSImage)

For instance, adversaries have been noted embedding payloads within or as an overlay of seemingly benign binaries. (Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Instances have also been recorded where adversaries nest payloads, such as executables and run-only scripts, within a file of the same type. (Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021)

Embedded content can also serve as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads aimed at compromising benign system processes. (Citation: Trend Micro) These embedded and subsequently injected payloads may function as components of malware designed to deliver specific functionalities, including the encryption of C2 communications to support an orchestrator module. For example, an embedded module might be injected into default browsers, facilitating adversaries' ability to communicate over the network. (Citation: Malware Analysis Report ComRAT)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Services File Permissions Weakness

Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by services. Adversaries may use flaws in the permissions of Windows services to replace the binary that is executed upon service start. These service processes may automatically execute specific binaries as part of their functionality or to perform other actions. If the permissions on the file system directory containing a target binary, or permissions on the binary itself are improperly set, then the target binary may be overwritten with another binary using user-level permissions and executed by the original process. If the original process and thread are running under a higher permissions level, then the replaced binary will also execute under higher-level permissions, which could include SYSTEM.

Adversaries may use this technique to replace legitimate binaries with malicious ones as a means of executing code at a higher permissions level. If the executing process is set to run at a specific time or during a certain event (e.g., system bootup) then this technique can also be used for persistence.

**Technique:** Phishing

Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to induce a denial of service (DoS) by flooding a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This type of DoS attack can compromise the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) refers to the act of one or more systems transmitting a high volume of network packets directed at the service's network. Almost any network protocol is capable of being exploited for flooding purposes. While stateless protocols like UDP and ICMP are frequently utilized, stateful protocols such as TCP can also be employed.

Network flooding attacks are often executed using botnets targeting various networks and services. Large-scale botnets can produce considerable traffic from numerous systems distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries may possess the capability to establish and manage their own botnet infrastructure or may opt to rent access to an existing botnet to launch an attack. In extreme cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), an extensive number of systems may be leveraged to create the flood, allowing each one to transmit only a minimal amount of traffic sufficient to overwhelm the target network. In these situations, differentiating DDoS traffic from legitimate user traffic can prove to be exceptionally challenging. Botnets have been involved in some of the most notable DDoS flooding incidents, including the series of attacks in 2012 that targeted prominent US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Process Injection

Adversaries can inject code into existing processes to bypass process-based defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges. Process injection involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of another active process. By running code within the context of a different process, adversaries may gain access to that process's memory and system or network resources, along with the possibility of acquiring elevated privileges. Additionally, execution through process injection can evade detection from security tools, as the activity is concealed within a legitimate process.

There are various methods for injecting code into a process, many of which exploit legitimate functionalities. Such implementations are found across all major operating systems but tend to be specific to each platform.

More advanced examples might carry out multiple process injections to divide modules and further avoid detection, employing named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) methods as channels for communication.

**Technique:** SMB/Windows Admin Shares

Adversaries may utilize [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to access a remote network share via Server Message Block (SMB). Subsequently, the adversary can carry out actions as the user who is logged on.

SMB serves as a protocol for sharing files, printers, and serial ports among Windows systems within the same network or domain. This protocol allows adversaries to engage with file shares, facilitating lateral movement across a network. Implementations of SMB for Linux and macOS often utilize Samba.

Windows machines feature hidden network shares that are exclusively accessible to administrators, enabling remote file copying and a range of other administrative tasks. Examples of these network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`. Adversaries might exploit this technique alongside administrator-level [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely gain access to a networked system over SMB, (Citation: Wikipedia Server Message Block) engage with systems through remote procedure calls (RPCs), (Citation: TechNet RPC) transfer files, and execute transferred binaries via remote Execution. Attack description

An attacker exploits a vulnerability in the firmware of the Thunderbolt protocol on a computing device to alter the firmware of the Thunderbolt controller. This manipulation targets weaknesses in the implementation of authorization and verification techniques embedded within Thunderbolt's protective measures. Once the adversary has physical access to the intended device, they perform advanced firmware manipulation on the Thunderbolt controller's SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) flash using a SPI Programming device and an external Thunderbolt device, often while the target device is in the booting phase. If this manipulation is successful, the attacker gains the ability to alter memory, circumvent authentication processes, impersonate identities and content, as well as extract data and memory from the compromised device. Currently, there are 7 significant vulnerabilities identified within the Thunderbolt protocol, with 9 distinct attack vectors as detailed in the Execution Flow.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Space after Filename Attackers can obscure a program's actual file type by altering a file's extension. For certain file formats (notably, this method does not apply to .app extensions), adding a space at the end of a filename affects how the operating system processes the file. For instance, consider a Mach-O executable file named evil.bin; when a user double-clicks it, Terminal.app will be launched, and the file will execute. However, if this file is renamed to evil.txt, a double-click by a user will open it in the default text editing application, preventing the binary from executing. On the other hand, if the file is renamed to evil.txt (with a space included at the end), then upon double-clicking, the operating system identifies the true file type and processes it accordingly, resulting in the binary being executed (Citation: Mac Backdoors are back). Malicious actors can exploit this characteristic to deceive users into double-clicking seemingly harmless files of any type, ultimately leading to the execution of malicious content.

Adversaries might engage in passive network sniffing to intercept and gather information regarding an environment, including authentication credentials transmitted across the network. Network sniffing involves utilizing a system's network interface to observe or capture data being sent via wired or wireless connections. **Technique:** Exploit Public-Facing Application

**Technique:** Steal Web Session Cookie

An attacker may obtain session cookies from web applications or services and utilize them to access these platforms as an authenticated user, circumventing the need for credentials. Typically, session cookies serve as authentication tokens once a user has logged into a website.

These cookies frequently remain valid for prolonged durations, even when the web application is not in active use. They can be located on disk, within the browser's process memory, and in network traffic directed to remote systems. Moreover, other applications on the target's device may also keep sensitive authentication cookies in memory (for instance, applications that authenticate with cloud services). The presence of session cookies can enable the circumvention of certain multi-factor authentication measures. (Citation: Pass The Cookie)

Numerous instances of malware have been documented that specifically target cookies from local web browsers. Attack Description

An attacker conducts activities aimed at identifying the operating system or firmware version of a remote target by probing a device, server, or platform with a specially crafted request intended to elicit responses that disclose information regarding the operating systems or firmware present in the environment. The detection of the operating system is feasible due to the variations in the implementations of common protocols (such as IP or TCP). Although these implementation differences do not undermine the compatibility of the protocol, they can be detected because the target will exhibit distinctive responses to particular probing actions that violate the semantic or logical rules governing packet construction for that protocol. Each operating system will react differently to the unusual input, which allows for the fingerprinting of OS behavior. This form of OS fingerprinting can differentiate between various operating system types and versions.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Access Token Manipulation Adversaries may modify access tokens to operate under a different user or system security context to perform actions and bypass access controls. Windows uses access tokens to determine the ownership of a running process. A user can manipulate access tokens to make a running process appear as though it is the child of a different process or belongs to someone other than the user that started the process. When this occurs, the process also takes on the security context associated with the new token. An adversary can use built-in Windows API functions to copy access tokens from existing processes; this is known as token stealing. These token can then be applied to an existing process (i.e. [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001)) or used to spawn a new process (i.e. [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002)). An adversary must already be in a privileged user context (i.e. administrator) to steal a token. However, adversaries commonly use token stealing to elevate their security context from the administrator level to the SYSTEM level. An adversary can then use a token to authenticate to a remote system as the account for that token if the account has appropriate permissions on the remote system.(Citation: Pentestlab Token Manipulation) Any standard user can use the runas command, and the Windows API functions, to create impersonation tokens; it does not require access to an administrator account. There are also other mechanisms, such as Active Directory fields, that can be used to modify access tokens.

**Technique:** Shortcut Modification

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to create a denial of service (DoS) by inundating a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This DoS attack can diminish the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) refers to the scenario where one or more systems direct a large quantity of network packets toward the network of the targeted service. Virtually any network protocol can be utilized for flooding purposes. Commonly, stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are employed, although stateful protocols such as TCP are also applicable.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are frequently executed using botnets. Extensive botnets have the capability to produce a considerable amount of traffic from systems dispersed throughout the global Internet. Adversaries might possess the means to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure, or they may opt to lease time on a pre-existing botnet for their attack. In extreme scenarios involving distributed DoS (DDoS), a vast number of systems can be leveraged to create the flood, allowing each one to send out only a minimal amount of traffic necessary to saturate the target network. In such instances, it becomes exceedingly challenging to differentiate DDoS traffic from that of legitimate clients. Notably, botnets have played a role in some of the most prominent DDoS flooding incidents, including the series of events in 2012 that targeted major banks in the United States. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

**Technique:** Brute Force

If an adversary successfully guesses the correct password but cannot log into a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they might alter their infrastructure to align with the victim's location, thereby circumventing those policies. **Technique:** SMB/Windows Admin Shares

Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SMB is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with file shares, allowing them to move laterally throughout a network. Linux and macOS implementations of SMB typically use Samba.

Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`. Adversaries may use this technique in conjunction with administrator-level [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely access a networked system over SMB,(Citation: Wikipedia Server Message Block) to interact with systems using remote procedure calls (RPCs),(Citation: TechNet RPC) transfer files, and run transferred binaries through remote Execution. Example execution techniques that rely on authenticated sessions over SMB/RPC are [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053), [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002), and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047). Adversaries can also use NTLM hashes to access administrator shares on systems with [Pass the Hash](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002) and certain configuration and patch levels.(Citation: Microsoft Admin Shares)
