ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder Adversaries can establish persistence by either adding a program to a startup folder or by referencing it through a Registry run key. When an entry is added to the "run keys" in the Registry or the startup folder, the associated program will execute upon user login. (Citation: Microsoft Run Key) These programs are executed within the user's context and operate at the permission level of the respective account. The following run keys are present by default on Windows systems: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Run keys may be located under various hives. (Citation: Microsoft Wow6432Node 2018)(Citation: Malwarebytes Wow6432Node 2016) The HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx key is also available, although it is not created by default on Windows Vista and later versions. Entries in the Registry run keys can directly reference programs or list them as dependencies. (Citation: Microsoft Run Key) For instance, one can load a DLL at logon using a "Depend" key with RunOnceEx: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil[.]dll" (Citation: Oddvar Moe RunOnceEx Mar 2018) Inserting a program into a startup folder will similarly lead to its execution when a user logs in. There exists a startup folder for individual user accounts, in addition to a system-wide startup folder that is checked for any user account login. The path to the startup folder for the current user is C:\Users\\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup. The path for the startup folder accessible by all users is C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp. The adversary assumes the security context of whichever browser process the proxy is injected into. Browsers typically create a new process for each tab that is opened and permissions and certificates are separated accordingly. With these permissions, an adversary could potentially browse to any resource on an intranet, such as [Sharepoint](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/002) or webmail, that is accessible through the browser and which the browser has sufficient permissions. ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Network Sniffing

Adversaries have the capability to passively monitor network traffic, enabling them to gather information about an environment, including authentication credentials transmitted across the network. Network sniffing involves utilizing the network interface of a system to observe or capture data that is transmitted over either a wired or wireless connection. An adversary might configure a network interface to operate in promiscuous mode, allowing access to data in transit, or employ span ports to obtain a larger volume of data.

Information acquired through this technique may consist of user credentials, particularly those conveyed via an insecure, unencrypted protocol. Methods for name service resolution poisoning, such as [Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001), can also be employed to intercept credentials for websites, proxies, and internal systems by redirecting traffic to the adversary.

Network sniffing can uncover configuration information, such as active services, version numbers, and other network attributes (e.g., IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) that are essential for subsequent [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) operations. It is likely that adversaries will also exploit network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to quietly gain further insight into the environment.

In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring services to sniff network traffic originating from virtual machines. For instance, AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap enable users to designate specific instances for traffic collection and particular targets for directing the gathered traffic. (Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) Frequently, a significant portion of this traffic is transmitted in cleartext because of TLS termination occurring at the load balancer level, which alleviates the burden of encrypting and decrypting traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) The adversary can subsequently employ exfiltration techniques such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account to gain access to the captured traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries may execute network captures utilizing [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands like `monitor capture`. (Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Path Interception through Search Order Hijacking Adversaries can deploy their malicious payloads by manipulating the search order utilized for loading other programs. Since certain programs may not invoke others using the complete file path, attackers can insert their own file into the directory where the calling program resides, leading the operating system to execute their malicious software upon the request of the initiating program. Search order hijacking takes place when an adversary exploits the sequence in which Windows seeks out programs that lack a specified path. In contrast to [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001) search order hijacking, the search sequence varies based on the execution method employed. (Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess) (Citation: Windows NT Command Shell) (Citation: Microsoft WinExec) Nevertheless, it is typical for Windows to first search the directory of the initiating program before checking the Windows system directory. An adversary identifying a program vulnerable to search order hijacking (i.e., one that does not define the path to an executable) can exploit this flaw by creating a program that bears the same name as the inadequately specified program and placing it in the directory of the initiating program. For instance, if "example.exe" executes "cmd.exe" with the command-line argument net user, an attacker may introduce a program named "net.exe" into the same directory as example.exe. Consequently, "net.exe" will be executed instead of the legitimate Windows system utility net. Furthermore, if an adversary adds a program named "net.com" to the same directory as "net.exe", the command cmd.exe /C net user will trigger "net.com" to run instead of "net.exe" due to the order of executable extensions established under PATHEXT. (Citation: Microsoft Environment Property) Search order hijacking is also frequently used for intercepting DLL loads and is discussed in [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001).

Attack description

Through the exploitation of how service accounts leverage Kerberos authentication with Service Principal Names (SPNs), the adversary obtains and subsequently cracks the hashed credentials of a service account target to exploit its privileges. The Kerberos authentication protocol centers around a ticketing system which is used to request/grant access to services and to then access the requested services. By extracting the local ticket and saving it disk, the adversary can brute force the hashed value to reveal the target account credentials.

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices using an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique to support follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By abusing features of common networking protocols that can determine the flow of network traffic (e.g. ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries may force a device to communicate through an adversary controlled system so they can collect information or perform additional actions.(Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For example, adversaries may manipulate victim DNS settings to enable other malicious activities such as preventing/redirecting users from accessing legitimate sites and/or pushing additional malware.(Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Adversaries may also manipulate DNS and leverage their position in order to intercept user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)).(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689)s can also be used to establish an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, deprecated, or weaker version of communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm.(Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Adversaries may also leverage the AiTM position to attempt to monitor and/or modify traffic, such as in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). Adversaries can setup a position similar to AiTM to prevent traffic from flowing to the appropriate destination, potentially to impair defenses and/or in support of a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to achieve a denial of service (DoS) by directing a large volume of network traffic at a specific target. This DoS assault can also impair the availability and operation of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) refers to instances where one or more systems generate a high volume of network packets aimed at the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be utilized for flooding purposes. While stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently employed, stateful protocols such as TCP may also be applicable.

Network flooding attacks against various networks and services are often executed using botnets. Extensive botnets can produce substantial traffic from a collection of systems distributed throughout the global Internet. Adversaries might possess the capabilities to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or may opt to lease resources on an existing botnet to launch an attack. In severe cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), the sheer number of systems involved in generating the flood means that each one needs to transmit only a minimal amount of traffic to create sufficient volume to overwhelm the target network. In such scenarios, differentiating DDoS traffic from that of legitimate clients becomes remarkably challenging. Some of the most notable DDoS flooding attacks have utilized botnets, including the series of events in 2012 that targeted prominent US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Services File Permissions Weakness

Adversaries can run their own malicious payloads by taking control of the binaries utilized by services. They may exploit vulnerabilities in the permissions of Windows services to substitute the binary that is activated at service startup. These service processes might inherently execute certain binaries as part of their operations or to carry out additional actions. If the file system directory holding a target binary, or the permissions on the binary itself, are incorrectly configured, a target binary could be replaced with another binary using user-level permissions and executed by the original process. Should the original process and thread be operating at a higher permission level, the substituted binary will also run with elevated permissions, potentially including SYSTEM.

Adversaries might employ this technique to swap out legitimate binaries for malicious versions as a method of executing code with higher permissions. If the executing process is programmed to run at a designated time or triggered by a specific event (such as system bootup), this technique can also facilitate persistence.

**Technique:** Brute Force

Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Adversaries may poison Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to position themselves between the communication of two or more networked devices. This activity may be used to enable follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol is used to resolve IPv4 addresses to link layer addresses, such as a media access control (MAC) address.(Citation: RFC826 ARP) Devices in a local network segment communicate with each other by using link layer addresses. If a networked device does not have the link layer address of a particular networked device, it may send out a broadcast ARP request to the local network to translate the IP address to a MAC address. The device with the associated IP address directly replies with its MAC address. The networked device that made the ARP request will then use as well as store that information in its ARP cache.

An adversary may passively wait for an ARP request to poison the ARP cache of the requesting device. The adversary may reply with their MAC address, thus deceiving the victim by making them believe that they are communicating with the intended networked device. For the adversary to poison the ARP cache, their reply must be faster than the one made by the legitimate IP address owner. Adversaries may also send a gratuitous ARP reply that maliciously announces the ownership of a particular IP address to all the devices in the local network segment.

The ARP protocol is stateless and does not require authentication. Therefore, devices may wrongly add or update the MAC address of the IP address in their ARP cache.(Citation: Sans ARP Spoofing Aug 2003)(Citation: Cylance Cleaver)

Adversaries may use ARP cache poisoning as a means to intercept network traffic. This activity may be used to collect and/or relay data such as credentials, especially those sent over an insecure, unencrypted protocol.(Citation: Sans ARP Spoofing Aug 2003)

Attack description

An attacker conducts operations aimed at identifying the operating system or firmware version of a remote target by probing a device, server, or platform with a carefully crafted request intended to elicit behavior that discloses information about the operating systems or firmware present in the environment. The detection of the Operating System is feasible due to the variations in the implementations of standard protocols (such as IP or TCP). Although these implementation differences do not compromise protocol compatibility, they can be detected because the target will react in distinct manners to certain probing actions that violate the semantic or logical principles of packet formation for a protocol. This method of OS fingerprinting can differentiate between types and versions of operating systems.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Kerberoasting

Adversaries can exploit a legitimate Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or intercept network traffic to acquire a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that might be susceptible to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110). (Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Service principal names (SPNs) serve to distinctly identify each instance of a Windows service. For authentication to occur, Kerberos mandates that SPNs be linked to at least one service logon account, which is designated specifically for running a service (Citation: Microsoft Detecting Kerberoasting Feb 2018). (Citation: Microsoft SPN)(Citation: Microsoft SetSPN)(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)(Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

Adversaries holding a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) can request one or multiple Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) service tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC). (Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) Some sections of these tickets may be encrypted using the RC4 algorithm, which means that the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the service account linked with the SPN acts as the private key and is, therefore, vulnerable to offline [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) attacks that could reveal plaintext credentials. (Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

This same activity could also be carried out using service tickets obtained from network traffic. (Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Compromised hashes may facilitate [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) through access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078). (Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)

**Technique:** Scheduled Task/Job

Adversaries might exploit the task scheduling capabilities to enable the initial or repeated execution of malicious software. All major operating systems provide utilities that allow for the scheduling of programs or scripts to run at a designated date and time. Additionally, a task can be arranged to run on a remote system, provided appropriate authentication is achieved (e.g., RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). To schedule a task on a remote system, it often requires membership in an administrative or similarly privileged group on that system. (Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries can leverage task scheduling to run applications at system startup or at predetermined intervals for persistence. These mechanisms can also be exploited to execute a process within the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). In a manner similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have been known to misuse task scheduling to potentially obfuscate one-time executions under the guise of a trusted system process. (Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Obfuscated Files or Information

Adversaries may seek to complicate the discovery or analysis of an executable or file by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its content while on the system or during transit. This behavior is frequently observed across various platforms and networks to bypass security defenses.

To avoid detection, payloads may be compressed, archived, or encrypted. These payloads can be utilized during Initial Access or at later stages to reduce the likelihood of detection. Occasionally, user interaction is necessary to open and [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Additionally, a user may need to enter a password to access a password-protected compressed or encrypted file supplied by the adversary. (Citation: Volexity PowerDuke November 2016) Adversaries might also employ compressed or archived scripts, including JavaScript.

Segments of files can be encoded to obscure the plain-text strings that would typically assist defenders in detection. (Citation: Linux/Cdorked.A We Live Security Analysis) Furthermore, payloads may be divided into multiple, seemingly harmless files that only exhibit malicious capabilities when they are reassembled. (Citation: Carbon Black Obfuscation Sept 2016)

Adversaries can also take advantage of [Command Obfuscation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/010) to conceal commands executed from payloads or directly through the [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059). They can utilize environment variables, aliases, characters, and other platform or language-specific semantics to evade signature-based detections and application control mechanisms. (Citation: FireEye Obfuscation June 2017)(Citation: FireEye Revoke-Obfuscation July 2017)(Citation: PaloAlto EncodedCommand March 2017)

Attack description

An attacker conducts activities aimed at identifying the operating system or firmware version of a remote target by probing a device, server, or platform with a specific probe intended to elicit responses that disclose information regarding the operating systems or firmware present in the environment. Detection of the operating system is feasible due to the variations in the implementations of common protocols (such as IP or TCP). Although these implementation variations do not lead to a loss of compatibility with the protocol, they can be detected since the target will react in distinct manners to particular probing activities that violate the semantic or logical principles of packet construction for a protocol. Various operating systems will respond uniquely to the irregular input, forming the basis for fingerprinting the OS behavior. This method of OS fingerprinting is capable of differentiating between types and versions of operating systems.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Network Sniffing

Adversaries have the capability to passively monitor network traffic to obtain information about an environment, which may include authentication credentials transmitted over the network. Network sniffing involves utilizing the network interface of a system to observe or capture data sent through either a wired or wireless connection. An attacker might configure a network interface to operate in promiscuous mode to gain passive access to data traversing the network or employ span ports to gather a broader range of information.

The data acquired through this method can encompass user credentials, particularly those transmitted via insecure, unencrypted protocols. Techniques such as [Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001) can also be implemented to intercept credentials for websites, proxies, and internal systems by rerouting traffic to an adversary.

Network sniffing can uncover configuration specifics, including running services, version numbers, and other network properties (e.g., IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) that are essential for later [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) operations. It is probable that adversaries will also leverage network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to passively gather additional insights about the environment.

In cloud environments, adversaries may still utilize traffic mirroring services to capture network traffic from virtual machines. Examples include AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap, which allow users to designate specific instances to collect traffic from and particular targets to which the gathered traffic is sent. (Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) Frequently, a significant portion of this traffic will be in cleartext due to TLS termination occurring at the load balancer level, which alleviates the load of encrypting and decrypting traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) Subsequently, adversaries can apply exfiltration techniques, such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account, to access the sniffed traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries might execute network captures utilizing [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands like `monitor capture`. (Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Token Impersonation/Theft

Adversaries may replicate and then impersonate the token of another user to elevate privileges and circumvent access controls. For instance, an adversary might use `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx` to replicate an existing token (Citation: DuplicateToken function). Subsequently, the replicated token can be utilized with `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` to enable the calling thread to adopt the security context of a logged on user, or with `SetThreadToken` to allocate the impersonated token to a specific thread.

An adversary might engage in [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) when they wish to assign the duplicated token to a particular, existing process. For example, this tactic could be advantageous when the targeted user has a non-network logon session active on the system.

Alternatively, if an adversary chooses to employ a duplicated token to spawn a new process instead of linking to an existing one, they can also utilize [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002) through `CreateProcessWithTokenW` or `CreateProcessAsUserW`. It is important to note that [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) differs from [Make and Impersonate Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/003) in that it involves the duplication of an existing token rather than the creation of a new one.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Path Interception through Search Order Hijacking Adversaries may deploy their malicious payloads by manipulating the search order used to load various programs. Certain applications do not utilize the full path when calling other programs, allowing adversaries to insert their own file into the directory of the calling program, which leads the operating system to execute their malicious software at the behest of the calling program. Search order hijacking transpires when an adversary exploits the sequence in which Windows looks for programs that lack a specified path. In contrast to [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001) search order hijacking, this search order varies based on the method employed to execute the program. (Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess) (Citation: Windows NT Command Shell) (Citation: Microsoft WinExec) Nevertheless, it is typical for Windows to first search in the directory of the initiating program before proceeding to the Windows system directory. An adversary recognizing a program susceptible to search order hijacking (i.e., a program that fails to specify the path to an executable) can exploit this weakness by creating a program mirroring the name of the improperly specified program and placing it in the directory of the initiating program. For instance, if "example.exe" invokes "cmd.exe" with the command-line argument net user, an adversary might position a program named "net.exe" within the same directory as example.exe. As a result, "net.exe" will execute in lieu of the Windows system utility net. Furthermore, if an adversary places a program called "net.com" in the same directory as "net.exe," then cmd.exe /C net user will run "net.com" instead of "net.exe," due to the executable extension order specified by PATHEXT. (Citation: Microsoft Environment Property) Search order hijacking is also frequently employed for the manipulation of DLL loads and is discussed in [DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/001).

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Impair Command History Logging Adversaries may disable command history logging to conceal the commands executed on an infiltrated system. Multiple command interpreters maintain a record of the commands entered by users in their terminal, allowing them to review their actions. On Linux and macOS, command history is stored in a file referenced by the environment variable HISTFILE. When a user logs off from the system, this data is written to a file in the user's home directory named ~/.bash_history. The HISTCONTROL environment variable determines which commands are saved by the history command and subsequently written to the ~/.bash_history file upon user logout. While HISTCONTROL is not present by default on macOS, users can configure it, and it will be acknowledged. The `HISTFILE` environment variable is also utilized in certain ESXi systems. (Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) To obstruct the logging of commands, adversaries might clear the history environment variable (unset HISTFILE) or set the command history size to zero (export HISTFILESIZE=0). Furthermore, HISTCONTROL can be adjusted to disregard commands that begin with a space by setting it to "ignorespace". It can also be configured to ignore duplicate commands by specifying "ignoredups". In several Linux distributions, this is set by default to "ignoreboth", which encompasses both of the aforementioned examples. Consequently, “ ls” will not be recorded, whereas “ls” will be saved in history. Adversaries can exploit this behavior to operate without leaving behind evidence by simply prefixing a space to all their terminal commands. On Windows systems, the PSReadLine module logs commands from all PowerShell sessions and saves them to a file ($env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt by default). Adversaries might redirect these logs to another location using Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySavePath {File Path}, which will prevent ConsoleHost_history.txt from receiving log entries. Additionally, logging to this file can be disabled altogether with the PowerShell command Set-PSReadlineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing. (Citation: Microsoft PowerShell Command History)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell command audit)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell Command History Forensics) Adversaries may also utilize a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on networking devices to turn off historical command logging (e.g. no logging).

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Using the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique, adversaries may seek to insert themselves between multiple networked devices to facilitate subsequent actions such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By exploiting the functionalities of widely-used networking protocols that dictate network traffic flow (e.g., ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries can compel a device to route its communications through a system they control, allowing them to gather information or execute further operations. (Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For instance, adversaries may alter the DNS settings of their victims to facilitate other malicious activities, which could include redirecting users away from legitimate websites or deploying additional malware. (Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Additionally, adversaries can manipulate DNS to exploit their position for intercepting user credentials, which encompasses access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)). (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689) techniques can also be employed to establish an AiTM position, for instance, by negotiating a less secure, outdated, or weaker version of a communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm. (Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Moreover, adversaries might utilize their AiTM position to monitor and/or alter traffic, as seen in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). They can establish a position akin to AiTM to obstruct traffic from reaching its intended destination, potentially undermining defenses or facilitating a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

Attack description

A malicious actor generates a deceptive yet operational session credential to obtain or take over access to a service. Session credentials enable users to authenticate themselves to a service following an initial login without having to resend their authentication details (typically a username and password) with each communication. Should an attacker manage to fabricate valid session credentials, they could potentially circumvent authentication or exploit another authenticated user's session. This type of attack is distinct from Reuse of Session IDs and Session Sidejacking attacks in that, in the latter scenarios, an attacker employs a prior or existing credential unchanged, whereas in a forging attack, the perpetrator must produce their own credential, which may, however, be derived from previously observed credentials.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Network Sniffing

Adversaries may engage in passive network traffic sniffing to obtain information regarding an environment, which includes authentication credentials transmitted across the network. Network sniffing is defined as the practice of utilizing a system's network interface to observe or collect data sent over wired or wireless connections. An adversary could configure a network interface to operate in promiscuous mode to access data in transit passively, or employ span ports to obtain a broader volume of data.

Data acquired through this technique may consist of user credentials, particularly those transmitted via insecure, unencrypted protocols. Methods for name service resolution poisoning, such as [Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001), can also be utilized to intercept credentials to websites, proxies, and internal systems by rerouting traffic to an adversary.

Network sniffing can disclose configuration information, including running services, version numbers, and other network attributes (e.g., IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) that are critical for later [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) operations. Adversaries are likely to employ network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to passively gather further insights regarding the environment.

In cloud environments, adversaries may still exploit traffic mirroring services to sniff network traffic from virtual machines. For instance, services like AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap enable users to designate specific instances for traffic collection and specify targets for redirecting the acquired traffic. (Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) A significant portion of this traffic may be unencrypted due to TLS termination at the load balancer level, which alleviates the burden of encrypting and decrypting the traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) The adversary may subsequently utilize exfiltration techniques, such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account, to gain access to the captured traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries might execute network captures employing [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands like `monitor capture`. (Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software)

**Technique:** Embedded Payloads

Adversaries have the capability to embed payloads within other files, thereby obscuring malicious content from security measures. Files that appear innocuous (such as scripts and executables) may be exploited to carry and disguise harmful payloads and data. In certain instances, the use of embedded payloads can also allow adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) without affecting execution controls, like digital signatures and notarization tickets. (Citation: Sentinel Labs)

Adversaries can incorporate payloads into a range of file formats to effectively hide them. (Citation: Microsoft Learn) This method resembles [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003); however, it does not require integrating malicious content into specific bytes or patterns associated with legitimate digital media formats. (Citation: GitHub PSImage)

For instance, it has been noted that adversaries have embedded payloads within or as an overlay of an otherwise harmless binary. (Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Additionally, adversaries have been seen nesting payloads (such as executables and run-only scripts) inside a file of the same type. (Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021)

Embedded content can also serve as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads that infect benign system processes. (Citation: Trend Micro) These payloads, once embedded and injected, may function as components of malware designed to offer specific capabilities, such as encrypting C2 communications in conjunction with an orchestrator module. For example, an embedded module might be injected into default web browsers, enabling adversaries to communicate over the network. (Citation: Malware Analysis Report ComRAT)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Space after Filename Threat actors can obscure the actual filetype of a program by altering the file extension. For specific file types (notably, this does not apply to .app extensions), adding a space at the end of a filename will affect how the operating system processes the file. For instance, consider a Mach-O executable file named evil.bin; when a user double clicks it, Terminal.app will launch and execute the file. If this file is renamed to evil.txt, double clicking it will open with the default text editor (preventing the binary from executing). Conversely, if the filename is modified to evil.txt (with a space at the end), double clicking it will prompt the OS to identify the true file type and handle it accordingly, causing the binary to execute (Citation: Mac Backdoors are back). This technique can be exploited by adversaries to deceive users into double clicking seemingly harmless files of any type, eventually leading to the execution of malicious content.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Services File Permissions Weakness

Adversaries can run their own malicious payloads by taking control of the binaries utilized by services. They may exploit vulnerabilities in the permissions of Windows services to substitute the binary that is triggered when the service starts. These service processes might automatically run certain binaries as part of their intended functionality or to carry out additional operations. If the permissions on the file system directory housing a target binary, or the permissions on the binary itself, are incorrectly configured, the target binary can be overwritten with another binary using user-level permissions and executed by the original process. When the original process and thread operate with elevated permissions, the substituted binary will also run with those higher-level permissions, potentially including SYSTEM.

Using this technique, adversaries can swap legitimate binaries for malicious ones, allowing them to execute code with elevated permissions. If the process is scheduled to run at a particular time or triggered by a specific event (for example, system startup), this technique can also serve as a method for persistence.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Token Impersonation/Theft

Threat actors may replicate and subsequently impersonate the token of another user to elevate their privileges and circumvent access controls. For instance, an adversary can use `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx` to replicate an existing token (Citation: DuplicateToken function). This replicated token can then be utilized with `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` to enable the calling thread to adopt the security context of a logged-on user, or with `SetThreadToken` to link the impersonated token to a specific thread.

An adversary might engage in [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) when they aim to attach the duplicated token to a particular existing process. This technique can be particularly beneficial when the target user is logged into a non-network session on the system.

In cases where an adversary opts to employ a duplicated token for the creation of a new process rather than linking it to an existing one, they can also utilize [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002) via `CreateProcessWithTokenW` or `CreateProcessAsUserW`. Additionally, [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) is differentiated from [Make and Impersonate Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/003) as it pertains to the replication of an existing token instead of the creation of a new token.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by directly sending a high-volume of network traffic to a target. This DoS attack may also reduce the availability and functionality of the targeted system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001)s are when one or more systems are used to send a high-volume of network packets towards the targeted service's network. Almost any network protocol may be used for flooding. Stateless protocols such as UDP or ICMP are commonly used but stateful protocols such as TCP can be used as well.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct network flooding attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global Internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for distributed DoS (DDoS), so many systems are used to generate the flood that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to saturate the target network. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS flooding attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Exploit Public-Facing Application

Adversaries might seek to take advantage of vulnerabilities in an Internet-facing host or system as a means to gain initial access to a network. Such a vulnerability could manifest as a software defect, a transient issue, or an improper configuration.

Typically, the applications being exploited include websites or web servers, but they may also encompass databases (such as SQL), common services (like SMB or SSH), protocols for managing and administering network devices (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any system with open sockets accessible via the Internet. (Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) In the context of ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may target exposed OpenSLP services; they may also exploit VMware vCenter servers that are publicly accessible. (Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the nature of the vulnerability being leveraged, this may also involve [Exploitation for Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

When an application is hosted on cloud infrastructure or is encapsulated within containers, exploiting it could result in the compromise of the underlying instance or container. This may provide adversaries a route to access cloud or container APIs (for example, through the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit access to the container host via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or exploit inadequate identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and associated appliances, specifically aiming at devices that lack robust host-based protections. (Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For both websites and databases, the most prevalent web-based vulnerabilities are outlined in the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25. (Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Impair Command History Logging Adversaries can disable command history logging to conceal the commands executed on a compromised system. Numerous command interpreters maintain a record of the commands that users enter in their terminal, allowing users to review their previous actions. In Linux and macOS environments, command history is stored in a file referenced by the environment variable HISTFILE. When a user logs out, this data is written to a file located in the user's home directory, named ~/.bash_history. The HISTCONTROL environment variable determines what commands are preserved by the history command and subsequently saved into the ~/.bash_history file upon user logout. Although HISTCONTROL is not set by default on macOS, users can configure it, and the setting will be honored. The `HISTFILE` environment variable is similarly utilized in certain ESXi systems. (Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) To obstruct command logging, adversaries can remove the history environment variable (unset HISTFILE) or set the command history size to zero (export HISTFILESIZE=0). Furthermore, HISTCONTROL can be adjusted to disregard commands that begin with a space by changing its value to "ignorespace". Additionally, it may be configured to ignore duplicate commands by assigning it the value "ignoredups". In some Linux distributions, the default setting is "ignoreboth", which encompasses both previous configurations. Consequently, “ ls” will not be recorded, but “ls” will be logged. Adversaries can exploit this functionality to operate without leaving any traces by simply starting all their terminal commands with a space. On Windows systems, the PSReadLine module logs commands from all PowerShell sessions and saves them to a file, which is by default located at $env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt. Adversaries have the ability to modify the location where these logs are stored by using the command Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySavePath {File Path}. This action will prevent ConsoleHost_history.txt from receiving any logs. Additionally, it is feasible to disable the logging to this file entirely by executing the PowerShell command Set-PSReadlineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing. (Citation: Microsoft PowerShell Command History)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell command audit)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell Command History Forensics) Adversaries might also utilize a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on networking equipment to turn off historical command logging (for instance, no logging).

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Weakness in File Permissions of Services

Adversaries have the capability to run their own malicious payloads by taking control of the binaries associated with services. They may exploit vulnerabilities in the permissions of Windows services to substitute the binary executed at service startup. These service processes often run specific binaries as part of their normal operations or to carry out additional tasks. If the permissions on the file system directory that houses a target binary, or the permissions on the binary itself, are incorrectly configured, it becomes possible for the target binary to be replaced with another binary using user-level permissions and executed by the original process. If the original thread and process operate under elevated permissions, the substituted binary will execute at that higher permission level, which might include SYSTEM access.

Adversaries can leverage this technique to swap out legitimate binaries for malicious ones, allowing them to execute code with elevated permissions. Furthermore, if the process is programmed to run at a specific time or triggered by a particular event (such as system boot), this technique can also serve as a method for achieving persistence.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Service Exhaustion Flood

Adversaries may exploit various network services offered by systems to execute a denial of service (DoS) attack. While the availability of DNS and web services is frequently targeted, other services can also fall victim. (Citation: Arbor AnnualDoSreport Jan 2018) Web server software is susceptible to attacks via numerous methods, some broadly applicable and others that are unique to the specific software providing the service.

A notable example of this attack type is the simple HTTP flood, in which an adversary inundates a web server with a high volume of HTTP requests, thereby overwhelming it and/or the application operating on it. This flood attack hinges on sheer volume to meet its goal, depleting any of the various resources necessary for the victim software to deliver the service. (Citation: Cloudflare HTTPflood)

Another variant, referred to as an SSL renegotiation attack, exploits a feature within the SSL/TLS protocol. The SSL/TLS protocol suite incorporates methods for the client and server to agree upon an encryption algorithm for future secure connections. When SSL renegotiation is enabled, a request can be initiated to renegotiate the cryptographic algorithm. In a renegotiation attack, the adversary first establishes an SSL/TLS connection and then makes a series of renegotiation requests. Given that cryptographic renegotiation incurs a significant computational cost, executing this in high volume can adversely affect the availability of the service. (Citation: Arbor SSLDoS April 2012)

Adversary Context in ATT&CK **Technique:** Browser Session Hijacking Attackers can exploit security flaws and the fundamental features of browser applications to alter content, influence user activities, and capture data as part of various browser session hijacking strategies. (Citation: Wikipedia Man in the Browser) One concrete instance is when an attacker injects malicious software into a browser, allowing them to access a user's cookies, HTTP sessions, and SSL client certificates, thereby utilizing the browser to gain entry into an authenticated intranet. (Citation: Cobalt Strike Browser Pivot) (Citation: ICEBRG Chrome Extensions) To perform browser-based actions such as pivoting, certain process privileges may be necessary, including SeDebugPrivilege and/or high-integrity or administrator rights. In another scenario, an attacker reroutes browser traffic from their own browser through the user's, by configuring a proxy that redirects web traffic. This configuration does not modify the user's traffic, and the proxy connection can be terminated immediately after the browser is closed. The attacker takes on the security context of the browser process into which the proxy is injected. Typically, browsers generate a new process for each tab opened, separating permissions and certificates accordingly. With these permissions, an attacker could potentially access any resource on an intranet, such as [SharePoint](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/002) or webmail, that is reachable through the browser and for which the browser has adequate permissions. Browser pivoting may also circumvent security measures provided by two-factor authentication. (Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

**Technique:** Pass the Hash

Adversaries can utilize stolen password hashes to execute "pass the hash" attacks, enabling lateral movement within an environment while circumventing standard system access controls. Pass the hash (PtH) serves as a method for authenticating as a user without requiring the cleartext password of that user. This approach skips the conventional authentication processes which necessitate a cleartext password, directly accessing the phase of authentication that employs the password hash.

In the execution of PtH, valid password hashes for the targeted account are acquired through a [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) technique. The gathered hashes are then employed with PtH to authenticate as the specified user. Upon successful authentication, PtH can be leveraged to carry out operations on both local and remote systems.

Additionally, adversaries may exploit stolen password hashes to perform "overpass the hash." This technique, akin to PtH, involves using a password hash for user authentication while also utilizing the password hash to generate a legitimate Kerberos ticket. Subsequently, this ticket may be used to conduct [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. (Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Services Registry Permissions Weakness Adversaries can execute their own malicious payloads by taking control of the Registry entries associated with services. Vulnerabilities in the permissions for Registry keys tied to services may allow adversaries to redirect the intended executable to one they manage, thus executing their own code when the service initiates. Windows retains local service configuration details in the Registry at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. The data found within a service's Registry keys can be adjusted to alter a service's execution parameters using tools like the service controller, sc.exe, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001), or [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075). Access to these Registry keys is regulated through access control lists and user permissions. (Citation: Registry Key Security)(Citation: malware_hides_service) If user and group permissions are not correctly configured, permitting access to the Registry keys for a service, adversaries might modify the service's binPath/ImagePath to direct it to an alternate executable under their control. Consequently, when the service is started or restarted, the adversary-controlled program will run, enabling the adversary to attain persistence and/or escalate privileges to the account context under which the service is set to operate (local/domain account, SYSTEM, LocalService, or NetworkService). Adversaries may also manipulate additional Registry keys within the service’s Registry hierarchy. For instance, the FailureCommand key could be modified so that the service executes in an elevated context whenever it fails or is deliberately compromised. (Citation: Kansa Service related collectors)(Citation: Tweet Registry Perms Weakness) The Performance key holds the name of a driver service's performance DLL along with the names of several exported functions from that DLL. (Citation: microsoft_services_registry_tree) If the Performance key does not already exist and an adversary-controlled user possesses the Create Subkey permission, adversaries could create the Performance key within the service’s Registry tree to link to a malicious DLL. (Citation: insecure_reg_perms) Additionally, adversaries can introduce the Parameters key, which has the potential to reference paths to malicious driver files. This technique has been recognized as a method of exploitation by configuring DLL file paths within the Parameters key of a particular service's registry setup. By positioning and configuring the Parameters key to reference a harmful DLL, adversaries can guarantee that their code is persistently loaded whenever the corresponding service or library is activated. For example, the registry path (Citation: MDSec) HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\WinSock2\Parameters (Citation: hexacorn)(Citation: gendigital) includes the AutodiaDLL value, which indicates the DLL to be loaded for autodial functionality. An adversary could change the AutodiaDLL to point to a compromised or malicious DLL: "AutodialDLL"="c:\temp\foo.dll" This guarantees persistence, as it results in the DLL (in this example, foo.dll) being loaded each time the Winsock 2 library is called.

**Technique:** Service Exhaustion Flood

Adversaries may focus on various network services offered by systems to execute a denial of service (DoS) attack. While DNS and web services are frequently targeted, other services have also been affected. (Citation: Arbor AnnualDoSreport Jan 2018) There are multiple methods through which web server software can be compromised; some techniques are broadly applicable, while others are tailored to specific software implementations.

A prominent example of this attack method is the simple HTTP flood, where an adversary inundates a web server with numerous HTTP requests, thereby overwhelming both the server and any applications operating on it. This form of flood depends on sheer volume to achieve its goal, depleting the various resources necessary for the victim software to deliver the service. (Citation: Cloudflare HTTPflood)

Another variant, termed an SSL renegotiation attack, exploits a feature inherent in the SSL/TLS protocol. The SSL/TLS suite encompasses mechanisms that allow the client and server to mutually agree on an encryption algorithm for future secure connections. When SSL renegotiation is enabled, there exists the possibility to request a change in the cryptographic algorithm. During a renegotiation attack, the adversary initiates an SSL/TLS connection and subsequently submits a series of renegotiation requests. As the cryptographic renegotiation demands a considerable amount of computational resources, executing this in high volume can adversely affect the availability of the service. (Citation: Arbor SSLDoS April 2012)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Space after Filename Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of a file. With certain file types (specifically this does not work with .app extensions), appending a space to the end of a filename will change how the file is processed by the operating system. For example, if there is a Mach-O executable file called evil.bin, when it is double clicked by a user, it will launch Terminal.app and execute. If this file is renamed to evil.txt, then when double clicked by a user, it will launch with the default text editing application (not executing the binary). However, if the file is renamed to evil.txt (note the space at the end), then when double clicked by a user, the true file type is determined by the OS and handled appropriately and the binary will be executed (Citation: Mac Backdoors are back). Adversaries can use this feature to trick users into double clicking benign-looking files of any format and ultimately executing something malicious.

**Technique:** Process Injection

Adversaries may utilize code injection into processes to bypass defenses that are based on processes and potentially increase their privileges. Process injection refers to the execution of arbitrary code within the address space of another active process. By running code in the context of a different process, attackers might gain access to the memory of that process, system/network resources, and possibly escalate their privileges. Furthermore, execution through process injection can avoid detection by security solutions, as the activity appears to be part of a legitimate process.

There are various methods for injecting code into a process, many of which exploit legitimate functionalities. These techniques are present across all major operating systems, although they tend to be specific to each platform.

More advanced examples may utilize multiple process injections to segment modules and enhance evasion from detection, using named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms as a channel for communication.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Steal Web Session Cookie

An adversary has the capability to capture session cookies from web applications or services, allowing them to access those web applications or Internet services as an authenticated user without the need for credentials. Web applications and services typically utilize session cookies as authentication tokens after a user successfully logs into a website.

These cookies often remain valid for extended durations, even when the web application is not being actively utilized. They can be located on disk, within the browser's process memory, and in network traffic directed to remote systems. Furthermore, other applications running on the targeted machine may also retain sensitive authentication cookies in memory (for example, applications that authenticate with cloud services). Session cookies can enable adversaries to circumvent certain multi-factor authentication protocols. (Citation: Pass The Cookie)

Multiple instances of malware have been identified that specifically target cookies from web browsers on the local system. (Citation: Kaspersky TajMahal April 2019)(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019) Adversaries may additionally obtain cookies by injecting harmful JavaScript code into websites or by employing [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) to deceive victims into executing malicious JavaScript in their browsers. (Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)

There exist also open-source frameworks like `Evilginx2` and `Muraena` that can collect session cookies via a malicious proxy (such as [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557)), which can be established by an adversary and utilized in phishing operations. (Citation: Github evilginx2)(Citation: GitHub Mauraena)

Once an adversary secures a valid cookie, they can utilize the [Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004) technique to log into the associated web application.

**Technique:** Adversary-in-the-Middle

Adversaries might try to insert themselves between multiple networked devices by employing an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) tactic to facilitate subsequent actions like [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By taking advantage of the functionalities of widely used networking protocols that influence the direction of network traffic (such as ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries can compel a device to interact via a system they control, allowing them to gather data or execute further activities. (Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For instance, adversaries might alter the DNS settings of a victim to enable various malicious operations, including hindering or redirecting users from legitimate websites and/or distributing additional malware. (Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Additionally, adversaries may manipulate DNS and exploit their position to capture user credentials, which can include access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)). (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) Furthermore, [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689)s can be utilized to gain an AiTM position by negotiating a less secure, outdated, or weaker variant of a communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption method. (Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

In addition, adversaries can exploit the AiTM position in an effort to observe and/or alter traffic, as seen in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). They can establish a position akin to AiTM to obstruct traffic from reaching its intended destination, potentially undermining defenses and/or supporting a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

Attack description

By exploiting the way service accounts utilize Kerberos authentication with Service Principal Names (SPNs), the attacker gains access to and subsequently cracks the hashed credentials of a targeted service account to leverage its privileges. The Kerberos authentication protocol is built around a ticketing system that facilitates the request and granting of access to services, enabling access to the requested resources. As an authenticated user, the attacker can request a service ticket from Active Directory, which contains portions encrypted using RC4 with the private key associated with the authenticated account. By extracting the local ticket and storing it on disk, the attacker is able to perform a brute-force attack on the hashed value to uncover the credentials of the target account.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to achieve a denial of service (DoS) by directly transmitting a substantial volume of network traffic to a specific target. This type of DoS attack can also impair the availability and performance of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) refers to scenarios in which one or more systems direct a high volume of network packets toward the network of the targeted service. Almost any network protocol can be utilized for flooding purposes. While stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently employed, stateful protocols such as TCP are also applicable.

Network flooding attacks against various networks and services are often executed using botnets. Large-scale botnets are capable of generating an immense amount of traffic from systems distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries may possess the necessary resources to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure, or they may opt to rent access to an existing botnet to launch an attack. In severe cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), such an extensive number of systems may be employed to generate the flood that each system only needs to transmit a minimal quantity of traffic to create sufficient volume to overwhelm the target network. In these situations, differentiating DDoS traffic from legitimate client traffic becomes extremely challenging. Botnets have been instrumental in some of the most notable DDoS flooding incidents, such as the series of attacks in 2012 that targeted prominent US banking institutions. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Pass the Hash

Adversaries can leverage stolen password hashes to facilitate lateral movement within an environment, effectively circumventing standard system access controls through a method known as "passing the hash." Pass the hash (PtH) allows for user authentication without requiring access to the user's cleartext password. This technique avoids conventional authentication processes that necessitate a cleartext password and directly engages with the segment of the authentication that utilizes the password hash.

In executing PtH, valid password hashes for the targeted account are obtained using a [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) technique. These captured hashes are then employed with PtH to authenticate as the specified user. Upon successful authentication, PtH can be utilized to execute actions on both local and remote systems.

Additionally, adversaries may exploit stolen password hashes to "overpass the hash." This approach mirrors PtH in that it uses a password hash for user authentication but also employs that hash to generate a legitimate Kerberos ticket. This Kerberos ticket can subsequently be utilized to conduct [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. (Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Steal Web Session Cookie

An adversary may obtain session cookies from web applications or services and leverage them to access these applications or Internet services as an authenticated user without the need for credentials. Typically, web applications and services utilize session cookies as an authentication token subsequent to a user logging into a website.

Cookies frequently remain valid for prolonged durations, even when the web application is not being actively engaged. They can be located on disk, within the process memory of the browser, and in network traffic directed to remote systems. Furthermore, other applications on the target's machine may also save sensitive authentication cookies in memory (for instance, applications that authenticate with cloud services). Session cookies can facilitate the circumvention of certain multi-factor authentication protocols. (Citation: Pass The Cookie)

There are multiple instances of malware that specifically target cookies stored in web browsers on local systems. (Citation: Kaspersky TajMahal April 2019)(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019) Adversaries may also extract cookies by injecting harmful JavaScript into websites or utilizing [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) to deceive victims into executing malicious JavaScript within their browser. (Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)

Additionally, there exist open-source frameworks like `Evilginx2` and `Muraena` that can collect session cookies via a malicious proxy (e.g., [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557)), which can be established by an adversary for use in phishing campaigns. (Citation: Github evilginx2)(Citation: GitHub Mauraena)

Once an adversary secures a valid cookie, they can proceed to employ a [Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004) technique to log into the respective web application.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Network Sniffing

Adversaries can passively monitor network traffic to gather information about an environment, including authentication credentials transmitted across the network. Network sniffing involves utilizing a system's network interface to observe or intercept data sent over both wired and wireless connections. An adversary might configure a network interface to operate in promiscuous mode, enabling passive access to data in transit, or employ span ports to capture a greater volume of data.

Data obtained through this method may encompass user credentials, particularly those transmitted via insecure, unencrypted protocols. Name service resolution poisoning techniques, such as [Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001), could also be leveraged to seize credentials for websites, proxies, and internal systems by rerouting traffic to the adversary's control.

Network sniffing can unveil configuration specifics, including running services, version identifiers, and other network attributes (e.g., IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) that are crucial for subsequent [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) operations. It is likely that adversaries will also utilize network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to passively acquire further insights into the environment.

In cloud environments, adversaries may still exploit traffic mirroring services to eavesdrop on network traffic from virtual machines. For instance, services like AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap enable users to specify particular instances for traffic collection and designated targets for routing the gathered traffic to. (Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring) (Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring) (Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) A significant portion of this traffic may be in cleartext, due to TLS termination occurring at the load balancer level to alleviate the load of encrypting and decrypting traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring) (Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) The adversary can subsequently implement exfiltration techniques such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account to gain access to the intercepted traffic. (Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries may carry out network captures using commands from [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008), such as `monitor capture`. (Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) (Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software)

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by directly sending a high-volume of network traffic to a target. This DoS attack may also reduce the availability and functionality of the targeted system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001)s are when one or more systems are used to send a high-volume of network packets towards the targeted service's network. Almost any network protocol may be used for flooding. Stateless protocols such as UDP or ICMP are commonly used but stateful protocols such as TCP can be used as well.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct network flooding attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global Internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for distributed DoS (DDoS), so many systems are used to generate the flood that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to saturate the target network. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS flooding attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Kerberoasting

Adversaries can exploit a legitimate Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or intercept network traffic to acquire a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that may be susceptible to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110).(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Service principal names (SPNs) serve to distinctly identify each instance of a Windows service. For authentication to function, Kerberos mandates that SPNs be linked to at least one service logon account (an account specifically designated for running a service(Citation: Microsoft Detecting Kerberoasting Feb 2018)).(Citation: Microsoft SPN)(Citation: Microsoft SetSPN)(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)(Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

Individuals who hold a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) are capable of soliciting one or more Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC).(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) Certain segments of these tickets may be encrypted using the RC4 algorithm, implying that the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the service account tied to the SPN is utilized as the private key, rendering it vulnerable to offline [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) attacks that could potentially reveal plaintext credentials.(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016) (Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

This same action can be performed using service tickets acquired from network traffic.(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Decrypted hashes may facilitate [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) through access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
