ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Scheduled Task/Job

Adversaries can exploit task scheduling capabilities to enable either the initial or repeated execution of malicious code. All major operating systems include utilities that allow for the scheduling of programs or scripts to run at designated dates and times. Additionally, a task may be scheduled on a remote machine, assuming the necessary authentication is provided (for example, RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling tasks on remote systems typically necessitates that the user is part of an administrative or otherwise privileged group on the target system. (Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries might leverage task scheduling to run programs during system startup or at predetermined intervals for persistence. These mechanisms can also be exploited to execute a process within the context of a specified account, such as one possessing elevated permissions or privileges. In a manner similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have exploited task scheduling to obscure one-time executions under the guise of a trusted system process. (Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

**Technique:** SMB/Windows Admin Shares

Adversaries might leverage [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to connect with a remote network share via Server Message Block (SMB). Consequently, the adversary could execute actions under the context of the logged-in user.

SMB is a protocol utilized for sharing files, printers, and serial ports among Windows machines within the same network or domain. Through SMB, adversaries can engage with file shares, facilitating lateral movement across a network. Implementations of SMB in Linux and macOS typically utilize Samba.

Hidden network shares in Windows systems are exclusively accessible to administrators, enabling remote file copying and various other administrative tasks. Examples of these network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`. Adversaries may combine this technique with administrator-level [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to gain remote access to systems over SMB,(Citation: Wikipedia Server Message Block) interact with systems via remote procedure calls (RPCs),(Citation: TechNet RPC) transfer files, and execute transferred binaries through remote execution. Techniques for execution that depend on authenticated sessions over SMB/RPC include [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053), [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002), and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047). Additionally, adversaries can utilize NTLM hashes to access administrator shares on systems with [Pass the Hash](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002) and specific configuration and patch levels.(Citation: Microsoft Admin Shares)

Another illustration includes redirecting browser traffic from the adversary’s browser through the victim’s browser by establishing a proxy that reroutes web traffic. This method does not modify the user's traffic and can have the proxy connection terminated as soon as the browser is closed. The adversary takes on the security context of the browser process into which the proxy is integrated. Typically, web browsers initiate a new process for every tab opened, with permissions and certificates being segregated accordingly. With these permissions, an adversary could potentially navigate to any resource available on an intranet, including [Sharepoint](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/002) or webmail, provided that the browser has sufficient access rights. Browser pivoting may also circumvent security measures offered by two-factor authentication. (Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Service Exhaustion Flood

Adversaries may exploit various network services offered by systems to perform a denial of service (DoS) attack. While the availability of DNS and web services is frequently targeted, other services have also been subjected to such attacks. (Citation: Arbor AnnualDoSreport Jan 2018) Web server software can be compromised through numerous methods, some of which are broadly applicable, while others are tailored to the specific software facilitating the service.

A prime example of this attack method is the simple HTTP flood, where an adversary sends an overwhelming number of HTTP requests to a web server, aiming to incapacitate it and/or any applications that depend on it. This flood attack leverages sheer volume to achieve its goal, depleting the various resources that the victim software requires to operate the service. (Citation: Cloudflare HTTPflood)

Another variant is the SSL renegotiation attack, which exploits a feature within the SSL/TLS protocol. The SSL/TLS protocol suite incorporates mechanisms that allow the client and server to agree upon an encryption algorithm for future secure connections. When SSL renegotiation is activated, a request can be submitted to renegotiate the cryptographic algorithm. In this type of attack, the adversary initiates an SSL/TLS connection and subsequently issues multiple renegotiation requests. Since the cryptographic renegotiation incurs a significant computational cost, executing this in large quantities can adversely affect the service's availability. (Citation: Arbor SSLDoS April 2012)

**Technique:** Token Impersonation/Theft

Adversaries may replicate and subsequently impersonate an existing token from another user to elevate privileges and circumvent access controls. For instance, an adversary can replicate a current token utilizing `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx`. (Citation: DuplicateToken function) This token can then be employed with `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`, enabling the designated thread to take on the security context of a logged-on user, or with `SetThreadToken` to assign the duplicated token to a specific thread.

An adversary might engage in [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) when they intend to assign the duplicated token to a particular, existing process. This tactic may be advantageous if the target user possesses a non-network logon session on the machine.

In scenarios where an adversary prefers to utilize a duplicated token to initiate a new process instead of linking to an existing one, they can also apply [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002) via `CreateProcessWithTokenW` or `CreateProcessAsUserW`. It is important to note that [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) is different from [Make and Impersonate Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/003), as it pertains to the duplication of an existing token rather than the creation of a new one.

**Technique:** Password Spraying

Adversaries may use a single or small list of commonly used passwords against many different accounts to attempt to acquire valid account credentials. Password spraying uses one password (e.g. 'Password01'), or a small list of commonly used passwords, that may match the complexity policy of the domain. Logins are attempted with that password against many different accounts on a network to avoid account lockouts that would normally occur when brute forcing a single account with many passwords. (Citation: BlackHillsInfosec Password Spraying)

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when password spraying. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)

In order to avoid detection thresholds, adversaries may deliberately throttle password spraying attempts to avoid triggering security alerting. Additionally, adversaries may leverage LDAP and Kerberos authentication attempts, which are less likely to trigger high-visibility events such as Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625 that is commonly triggered by failed SMB connection attempts.(Citation: Microsoft Storm-0940)

A malicious actor generates a counterfeit yet operational session credential to acquire or take over access to a service. Session credentials enable users to authenticate themselves to a service after the initial login without the need to retransmit their authentication data (typically a username and password) with each interaction. Should an attacker succeed in fabricating legitimate session credentials, they might circumvent authentication or exploit the session of another authenticated user. This method of attack is distinct from Session ID Reuse and Session Sidejacking attacks, as the latter involve the utilization of an existing credential without any alteration, whereas in a forging attack, the attacker must produce their own credential, which may be inspired by previously observed credentials.

(Citation: Wikipedia Man in the Browser) One notable instance occurs when an adversary injects code into a browser, enabling them to acquire cookies, HTTP sessions, and SSL client certificates from a user, thereby utilizing the browser as a means to access an authenticated intranet. The adversary adopts the security context of the browser process into which the proxy has been injected. Typically, browsers initiate a new process for each opened tab, resulting in permissions and certificates being managed separately. With these permissions, an adversary could potentially access any resource on an intranet, such as [Sharepoint](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/002) or webmail, that is available through the browser and for which the browser has adequate permissions. **Technique:** Embedded Payloads

Adversaries have the capability to conceal malicious content within other files, effectively embedding payloads to evade defensive measures. Files that appear benign, such as scripts and executables, can be exploited to transport and obscure harmful payloads and content. In certain instances, these embedded payloads may allow adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) by not affecting execution mechanisms like digital signatures and notarization tickets. (Citation: Sentinel Labs)

Payloads can be embedded by adversaries across a range of file formats to obscure their nature. (Citation: Microsoft Learn) This technique is akin to [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), though it does not entail embedding malicious content within specific byte patterns tied to legitimate digital media formats. (Citation: GitHub PSImage)

For instance, adversaries have been noted embedding payloads within or as an overlay on otherwise harmless binaries. (Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Additionally, there have been observations of adversaries nesting payloads, such as executables and run-only scripts, within files of the same type. (Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021)

Embedded content can also function as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads that infect innocent system processes. (Citation: Trend Micro) These injected payloads that were originally embedded may serve as modules of malware designed to offer specific functionalities, such as encrypting command and control communications in support of an orchestrator module. **Technique:** Services File Permissions Weakness

Adversaries can execute their own harmful payloads by taking control of the binaries associated with services. They may exploit vulnerabilities in the permissions of Windows services to substitute the binary that launches when the service starts. These service processes might automatically run designated binaries as part of their operations or to carry out other tasks. If the file system directory containing a targeted binary, or the permissions on the binary itself, are incorrectly configured, the target binary could be replaced with another binary using user-level permissions and then executed by the original process. Should the original process and thread operate with a higher privilege level, the substituted binary will also run with elevated permissions, which may include SYSTEM privileges.

Adversaries might utilize this method to swap out legitimate binaries for malicious ones as a way to execute code with elevated permissions. If the process executing is scheduled to run at a certain time or triggered by a particular event (for example, system bootup), this technique can also serve as a means of persistence.

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to induce a denial of service (DoS) by sending an excessive volume of network traffic directly to a target. This DoS attack can also impair the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or multiple systems are employed to transmit a high volume of network packets toward the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be utilized for flooding; however, stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently favored, although stateful protocols such as TCP are also applicable.

Network flooding attacks against various networks and services are often executed using botnets. Extensive botnets can create substantial traffic from devices distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries may possess the capability to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or opt to lease access to an existing botnet for conducting an attack. In extreme instances of distributed DoS (DDoS), an overwhelming number of systems can be mobilized to generate the flood, allowing each one to transmit only a minimal amount of traffic while still producing sufficient volume to overwhelm the target network. Under these conditions, differentiating DDoS traffic from legitimate user traffic becomes exceedingly challenging. Botnets have been instrumental in some of the most notable DDoS flooding attacks, including the series of incidents in 2012 that targeted major banks in the United States. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

**Technique:** Process Injection

Adversaries might inject code into running processes to bypass defenses that are based on process monitoring and potentially to escalate their privileges. Process injection is a technique for executing arbitrary code within the address space of another active process. By running code within the context of a different process, attackers may gain access to that process's memory, system or network resources, and possibly even elevated privileges. This method of execution may also avoid detection by security tools, as the activity is concealed within a legitimate process.

There are various methods for injecting code into processes, many of which exploit legitimate functionalities. These tactics are applicable across all major operating systems but tend to be specific to each platform.

More advanced examples may execute multiple process injections to compartmentalize modules and further evade detection, leveraging named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms as a means of communication.

By exploiting characteristics of widely-used networking protocols that dictate network traffic flow (e.g., ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries can coerce a device into routing its communications through a system they control, enabling them to gather data or execute further activities. For instance, adversaries might alter a victim's DNS settings to facilitate other malicious objectives such as diverting users from accessing legitimate websites and/or distributing additional malware. (Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1689) strategies can also be employed to achieve an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, outdated, or weaker version of a communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption method. (Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Additionally, adversaries might exploit the AiTM position to monitor and/or alter traffic, such as in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). They can establish a setup akin to AiTM to block traffic from reaching its intended destination, potentially undermining defenses and/or facilitating a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries might seek to achieve a denial of service (DoS) by flooding a target with a substantial volume of network traffic. This type of DoS attack can impair the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or more systems direct a high volume of network packets towards the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be employed for flooding; while stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP are frequently utilized, stateful protocols such as TCP are also applicable.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are often executed using botnets. Large-scale botnets can produce a considerable amount of traffic from devices distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries might possess the capability to establish and manage their own botnet infrastructure or may opt to lease access to an existing botnet for their attack. In extreme instances of distributed DoS (DDoS), the number of systems involved in generating the flood is so high that each system only needs to transmit a small volume of traffic to create sufficient bandwidth to overwhelm the target network. Under these conditions, differentiating DDoS traffic from that of legitimate clients becomes tremendously challenging. Some of the most notorious DDoS flooding attacks have been executed using botnets, such as the series of incidents in 2012 that targeted major US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Password Spraying

Adversaries may employ a single commonly used password or a limited selection of them against numerous accounts to gain valid credentials. This technique involves using one password (for instance, 'Password01') or a small group of widely recognized passwords that can comply with the domain's complexity requirements. By attempting logins with that password across various accounts within a network, adversaries aim to circumvent account lockouts that typically occur when brute forcing a single account with multiple passwords. (Citation: BlackHillsInfosec Password Spraying)

When conducting password spraying, management services that operate over frequently used ports are often targeted. The following services are commonly sought after:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

Beyond management services, adversaries might focus on "single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications that utilize federated authentication protocols," as well as email applications accessible from the outside, like Office 365. (Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)

To evade detection thresholds, adversaries often intentionally slow down their password spraying efforts to prevent triggering security alerts. Furthermore, they may utilize LDAP and Kerberos authentication attempts, as these are less likely to set off high-profile alerts such as the Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625, which is frequently activated by unsuccessful SMB connection attempts. (Citation: Microsoft Storm-0940)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Impair Command History Logging To conceal the commands executed on a compromised system, adversaries might impair command history logging. Various command interpreters maintain a record of the commands entered by users in their terminals, allowing users to review their previous actions. In Linux and macOS environments, command history is monitored in a file specified by the environment variable HISTFILE. When a user logs out of a system, this data is written to a file located in the user's home directory, specifically ~/.bash_history. The HISTCONTROL environment variable determines which commands should be retained by the history command and subsequently stored in the ~/.bash_history file upon user logout. While HISTCONTROL is not present by default on macOS, users have the option to configure it, and their settings will be acknowledged. Additionally, the `HISTFILE` environment variable is utilized in certain ESXi systems. (Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) Adversaries might eliminate the history environment variable by executing unset HISTFILE or configure the command history size to zero using export HISTFILESIZE=0 to inhibit command logging. Furthermore, HISTCONTROL can be set to disregard commands commencing with a space by adjusting it to "ignorespace". It can also be configured to overlook duplicate commands by assigning it the value "ignoredups". In certain Linux distributions, the default setting is "ignoreboth", encompassing both previous scenarios. Thus, a command like “ ls” would not be recorded, while “ls” would be logged by history. Adversaries can exploit this behavior to perform actions without leaving traces by simply prefixing a space to all terminal commands. In Windows environments, the PSReadLine module captures commands from all PowerShell sessions and logs them to a default file ($env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt). Adversaries might modify the storage location of these logs using Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySavePath {File Path}, preventing ConsoleHost_history.txt from receiving any logs. Moreover, it is feasible to disable logging to this file through the PowerShell command Set-PSReadlineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing. (Citation: Microsoft PowerShell Command History)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell command audit)(Citation: Sophos PowerShell Command History Forensics) Additionally, adversaries may utilize a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to turn off historical command logging (e.g. no logging).

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Process Injection

Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Process injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via process injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process. 

There are many different ways to inject code into a process, many of which abuse legitimate functionalities. These implementations exist for every major OS but are typically platform specific. 

More sophisticated samples may perform multiple process injections to segment modules and further evade detection, utilizing named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms as a communication channel.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Thread Execution Hijacking Adversaries may inject harmful code into compromised processes to circumvent process-based defenses and potentially increase privileges. Thread Execution Hijacking refers to the technique of executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate, active process. Typically, Thread Execution Hijacking is executed by suspending a currently running process, then unmapping or hollowing out its memory, which can subsequently be substituted with malicious code or a path to a DLL. Initially, a handle to the victim process is established using native Windows API functions such as OpenThread. Following this, the process can be suspended, modified to align with the injected code, and then resumed using SuspendThread, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, and finally ResumeThread in sequence. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) This technique closely resembles [Process Hollowing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012), but it focuses on an already existing process instead of initiating a process in a suspended state. Executing code within the context of another process may grant access to that process's memory, system or network resources, and potentially elevated privileges. Moreover, execution through Thread Execution Hijacking can also avoid detection by security solutions, as the execution occurs under the guise of a legitimate process.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Direct Network Flood

Adversaries may seek to induce a denial of service (DoS) by directly transmitting a substantial volume of network traffic to a chosen target. This type of DoS attack can diminish the availability and functionality of the affected system(s) and network. A [Direct Network Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/001) occurs when one or multiple systems are utilized to dispatch a high volume of network packets toward the network of the targeted service. Nearly any network protocol can be employed for flooding, with stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP being frequently utilized, though stateful protocols such as TCP are also applicable.

Network flooding attacks against services and networks are often carried out using botnets. Large-scale botnets can produce a considerable amount of traffic from systems distributed across the global Internet. Adversaries might possess the means to develop and manage their own botnet infrastructure or may opt to rent access to an existing botnet to execute an attack. In severe cases of distributed DoS (DDoS), an extensive number of systems can generate the flood, enabling each to send only a small amount of traffic while still achieving enough volume to overwhelm the target network. Under such conditions, it becomes extremely challenging to differentiate between DDoS traffic and legitimate client traffic. Some of the most notorious DDoS flooding attacks have involved botnets, including the series of incidents in 2012 that targeted prominent US banks. (Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Terminal Services DLL Adversaries may exploit Terminal Services components to maintain persistent access to systems. Microsoft Terminal Services, which was renamed to Remote Desktop Services in some Windows Server operating systems as of 2022, facilitates remote terminal connections to hosts. Through Terminal Services, servers can deliver a complete, interactive graphical user interface to clients via RDP. (Citation: Microsoft Remote Desktop Services) [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003) instances running as a "generic" process (e.g., svchost.exe) load the service's DLL file, with the path stored in a Registry key called ServiceDll. (Citation: Microsoft System Services Fundamentals) The termsrv.dll file, usually located in `%SystemRoot%\System32\`, serves as the default ServiceDll value for Terminal Services found in `HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\services\TermService\Parameters\`. To enable persistent access to compromised hosts, adversaries may alter and/or substitute the Terminal Services DLL. (Citation: James TermServ DLL) Changes made to this DLL could be intended to execute arbitrary payloads (while potentially preserving the standard termsrv.dll functionality) as well as to activate exploitable features of Terminal Services. For instance, an adversary might enable features such as concurrent [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001) sessions by either patching the termsrv.dll file or changing the ServiceDll value to direct to a DLL that enhances RDP capabilities. (Citation: Windows OS Hub RDP) (Citation: RDPWrap Github) On a non-server Windows operating system, this augmented functionality may also allow an adversary to bypass Terminal Services prompts that log out users or warn them when a new RDP session is initiated.

**Technique:** SMB/Windows Admin Shares

Adversaries may leverage [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to access a remote network share via Server Message Block (SMB). This allows the adversary to execute actions as the user who is currently logged in.

SMB serves as a protocol for sharing files, printers, and serial ports among Windows machines within the same network or domain. Adversaries can utilize SMB for interacting with file shares, enabling them to conduct lateral movements across a network. Implementations of SMB on Linux and macOS generally make use of Samba.

Hidden network shares exist on Windows systems, which are exclusively accessible to administrators, granting the capability for remote file copying and various administrative operations. Examples of such network shares include `C$`, `ADMIN$`, and `IPC$`. This technique may be employed by adversaries together with administrator-level [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely connect to a system on the network via SMB, (Citation: Wikipedia Server Message Block) allowing interaction with systems through remote procedure calls (RPCs), (Citation: TechNet RPC) file transfers, and the execution of transferred binaries through remote execution. Techniques for execution that depend on authenticated sessions over SMB/RPC include [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053), [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002), and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047). Furthermore, adversaries can exploit NTLM hashes to gain access to administrator shares on systems utilizing [Pass the Hash](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002) and specific configuration and patch levels. (Citation: Microsoft Admin Shares)

**Technique:** Brute Force

Adversaries can employ brute force methods to obtain access to accounts when they do not have knowledge of the passwords or when they have acquired password hashes. (Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) In situations where an adversary lacks the password for one or more accounts, they may methodically guess the password using an iterative or repetitive approach. (Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Password brute forcing can occur through interaction with a service that verifies the validity of those credentials or through offline attempts against previously obtained credential information, such as password hashes.

Credential brute forcing might occur at different stages throughout a breach. For instance, adversaries may try to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a compromised environment by utilizing information gained from other post-compromise activities like [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Additionally, adversaries might integrate brute forcing efforts with actions such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of their Initial Access strategy.

If an adversary successfully guesses the correct password but is unable to log in to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access controls, they may alter their infrastructure to align with the victim's location, thereby circumventing those controls. (Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** ARP Cache Poisoning

Adversaries may manipulate Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to insert themselves into the communication pathway between two or more networked devices. This tactic can facilitate subsequent actions like [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002).

The ARP protocol serves to translate IPv4 addresses into link layer addresses, such as media access control (MAC) addresses. Devices within a local network segment interact with one another using these link layer addresses. When a networked device lacks the link layer address for a specific device, it may issue a broadcast ARP request to the local network to convert the IP address into a MAC address. The device that owns the corresponding IP address responds directly with its MAC address. The networked device that initiated the ARP request will then utilize and store this information in its ARP cache.

An adversary may choose to passively monitor for an ARP request to corrupt the ARP cache of the requesting device. By replying with their own MAC address, the adversary misleads the victim into believing they are communicating with the legitimate networked device. To successfully poison the ARP cache, the adversary's reply must arrive more quickly than that of the true owner of the IP address. Additionally, adversaries might dispatch a gratuitous ARP reply, maliciously claiming ownership of a specific IP address to all devices on the local network segment.

As the ARP protocol is stateless and lacks authentication requirements, devices may mistakenly add or update the MAC address corresponding to an IP address in their ARP cache.

Adversaries may exploit ARP cache poisoning as a strategy to intercept network traffic, which can be used to gather and/or relay sensitive data such as credentials, particularly those transmitted over insecure, unencrypted protocols.

**Technique:** Token Impersonation/Theft

Adversaries may duplicate then impersonate another user's existing token to escalate privileges and bypass access controls. For example, an adversary can duplicate an existing token using `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx`.(Citation: DuplicateToken function) The token can then be used with `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` to allow the calling thread to impersonate a logged on user's security context, or with `SetThreadToken` to assign the impersonated token to a thread.

An adversary may perform [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) when they have a specific, existing process they want to assign the duplicated token to. For example, this may be useful for when the target user has a non-network logon session on the system.

[Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) is also distinct from [Make and Impersonate Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/003) in that it refers to duplicating an existing token, rather than creating a new one.

**Technique:** Credential Stuffing

Adversaries might exploit credentials acquired from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to access targeted accounts through credential overlap. Often, when a website or service is compromised, a significant number of username and password combinations are released online, revealing the user account credentials. This information can be advantageous for an adversary seeking to compromise accounts by leveraging the common behavior of users who tend to reuse passwords across both personal and business accounts.

Engaging in credential stuffing presents risks, as it may lead to a high number of authentication failures and account lockouts, contingent on the login failure policies of the organization.

Typically, management services operating over widely used ports are targeted during credential stuffing attacks. The following services are commonly aimed at:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)

Attack description

An attacker inserts a novel entry into the "run keys" within the Windows registry, enabling a selected application to launch automatically upon user login. This method allows the attacker to execute their executable file on the target machine using the permissions granted to the authorized user. Such an attack effectively facilitates the execution of persistent spyware, like a keylogger, on the user's device.

Attack description

An attacker creates a false but functional session credential in order to gain or usurp access to a service. Session credentials allow users to identify themselves to a service after an initial authentication without needing to resend the authentication information (usually a username and password) with every message. If an attacker is able to forge valid session credentials they may be able to bypass authentication or piggy-back off some other authenticated user's session. This attack differs from Reuse of Session IDs and Session Sidejacking attacks in that in the latter attacks an attacker uses a previous or existing credential without modification while, in a forging attack, the attacker must create their own credential, although it may be based on previously observed credentials.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Shortcut Modification

Adversaries may create or modify shortcuts that can execute a program during system boot or user login. Shortcuts or symbolic links are used to reference other files or programs that will be opened or executed when the shortcut is clicked or executed by a system startup process.

Adversaries may abuse shortcuts in the startup folder to execute their tools and achieve persistence.(Citation: Shortcut for Persistence ) Although often used as payloads in an infection chain (e.g. [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001)), adversaries may also create a new shortcut as a means of indirection, while also abusing [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the malicious shortcut appear as a legitimate program. Adversaries can also edit the target path or entirely replace an existing shortcut so their malware will be executed instead of the intended legitimate program.

Shortcuts can also be abused to establish persistence by implementing other methods. For example, LNK browser extensions may be modified (e.g. [Browser Extensions](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/001)) to persistently launch malware.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Token Impersonation/Theft

Adversaries can replicate and then impersonate an existing token belonging to another user to elevate privileges and circumvent access controls. For instance, an adversary may utilize `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx` to copy an existing token. (Citation: DuplicateToken function) This token can subsequently be employed with `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`, enabling the calling thread to take on the security context of a logged on user, or with `SetThreadToken` to allocate the impersonated token to a specific thread.

An adversary might engage in [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) when they wish to apply the duplicated token to a specific, existing process. For example, this technique may be advantageous when the target user is logged on to the system through a non-network session.

If an adversary intends to utilize a duplicated token to initiate a new process instead of linking to an existing one, they can further employ [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002) by using `CreateProcessWithTokenW` or `CreateProcessAsUserW`. It is important to note that [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001) is distinct from [Make and Impersonate Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/003) as it involves duplicating an existing token rather than generating a new one.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Services File Permissions Weakness

Adversaries might be able to run their own malicious payloads by taking control of the binaries utilized by services. They can exploit vulnerabilities in the permissions of Windows services to substitute the binary that is executed when the service starts. These service processes are designed to automatically run particular binaries as part of their operations or to carry out other tasks. If the permissions assigned to the file system directory housing a target binary, or the permissions on the binary itself, are misconfigured, then an attacker can overwrite the target binary with another binary using user-level permissions, which will be executed by the original process. Should the original process and thread operate under a higher level of permissions, the substituted binary will also run with elevated permissions, potentially reaching SYSTEM privileges.

Adversaries may leverage this technique to swap out legitimate binaries for malicious ones, allowing them to execute code with higher privileges. If the executing process is configured to run at a specific time or triggered by a certain event (for instance, during system bootup), this technique can also facilitate persistence.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Obfuscated Files or Information

Adversaries may seek to conceal an executable or file, making it challenging to detect or analyze by employing encryption, encoding, or other methods of obfuscation on the system or during transit. This tactic is frequently observed across various platforms and networks to bypass security measures.

Payloads may undergo compression, archiving, or encryption to evade detection. These payloads can be utilized during the Initial Access phase or later to reduce the likelihood of being identified. In some cases, a user's intervention might be necessary to access and [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Users may also have to provide a password to access a password-protected compressed/encrypted file supplied by the adversary. (Citation: Volexity PowerDuke November 2016) Additionally, adversaries might leverage compressed or archived scripts, including JavaScript.

Certain segments of files can be encoded to obscure plain-text strings that would otherwise assist defenders in detection. (Citation: Linux/Cdorked.A We Live Security Analysis) Payloads might also be divided into multiple, seemingly innocuous files, which only exhibit malicious behavior when reassembled. (Citation: Carbon Black Obfuscation Sept 2016)

Moreover, adversaries could exploit [Command Obfuscation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/010) to hide commands executed from payloads or directly through the [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059). They can utilize environment variables, aliases, special characters, and other platform/language specific conventions to circumvent signature-based detections and application control systems. (Citation: FireEye Obfuscation June 2017)(Citation: FireEye Revoke-Obfuscation July 2017)(Citation: PaloAlto EncodedCommand March 2017)

**Technique:** Exploitation for Stealth

Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities to evade detection by hiding activity, suppressing logging, or operating within trusted or unmonitored components. 

Adversaries may exploit a system or application vulnerability to avoid detection while maintaining access within an environment. Exploitation occurs when an adversary leverages a programming flaw to execute code in a manner that minimizes visibility or blends in with legitimate activity. 

Rather than directly disabling defenses, adversaries may use exploitation to circumvent monitoring and logging mechanisms. This can include abusing vulnerabilities in logging pipelines, security tools, or cloud infrastructure to evade audit trails, suppress alerts, or operate without generating telemetry. 

Adversaries may identify these opportunities through prior reconnaissance or by performing discovery of security controls after initial access. In some cases, vulnerabilities in SaaS or public cloud environments may be exploited to evade logging, obscure activity, or deploy infrastructure that remains hidden from standard monitoring tools.(Citation: Bypassing CloudTrail in AWS Service Catalog)(Citation: GhostToken GCP flaw)

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Phishing

Adversaries may utilize phishing messages to obtain access to victim systems. All varieties of phishing represent electronically delivered social engineering tactics. Phishing can be specifically directed, referred to as spearphishing. In spearphishing, the adversary focuses on a particular individual, organization, or sector. More broadly, adversaries can engage in non-targeted phishing, exemplified by mass malware spam campaigns.

Victims may receive emails from adversaries that contain harmful attachments or links, primarily aimed at executing malicious code on their systems. Phishing can also occur through third-party platforms, such as social media. Additionally, phishing may incorporate social engineering methods, like impersonating a trusted entity, along with evasive strategies such as altering or eliminating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts that are exploited to distribute messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)). (Citation: phishing-krebs)

Phishing messages may also instruct victims to call a specified phone number, directing them to visit a malicious URL, download malware, (Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install remote management tools that can be accessed by the adversary onto their device (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)). ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Weakness in Services File Permissions

Threat actors may leverage vulnerabilities in the permissions of Windows services to inject their own malicious payloads by taking control of the binaries utilized by those services. By exploiting incorrect permissions on the file system directory that holds a target binary, or on the binary itself, adversaries can substitute the original binary that is launched at service initiation. These service processes are designed to automatically run certain binaries as part of their operations or to execute additional tasks. When user-level permissions allow for it, the target binary can be replaced with another binary and subsequently run by the initial process. Should the original process and thread operate with elevated permissions, the substituted binary will execute at these higher permissions, potentially including SYSTEM privileges.

This technique enables adversaries to swap out legitimate binaries for malicious versions, thereby facilitating code execution with elevated permissions. If the process is configured to launch at designated times or specific events (such as system startup), this method can also be employed to achieve persistence.

A malicious actor generates a counterfeit yet operational session credential to obtain or take over access to a service. This attack is distinct from Session ID Reuse and Session Sidejacking attacks, as in the latter scenarios, an attacker exploits a prior or existing credential without alterations, whereas in a forging attack, the attacker must produce their own credential, which may be derived from previously monitored credentials.

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Access Token Manipulation Adversaries have the capability to alter access tokens, allowing them to function under a different user or system security context, thereby enabling actions that can bypass access controls. In the Windows environment, access tokens are utilized to identify the ownership of a process that is currently running. A user may adjust these access tokens to make it seem that a running process is a child of another process or is associated with a user other than the one who initiated the process. When this adjustment takes place, the process inherits the security context linked to the modified token. To execute this, an adversary can leverage built-in Windows API functions to duplicate access tokens from existing processes, a technique commonly referred to as token stealing. The acquired tokens can subsequently be applied to an already running process (i.e. [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001)) or utilized to launch a new process (i.e. [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002)). For token stealing to be successful, the adversary must already possess a privileged user context (i.e. administrator). Nevertheless, it is common for adversaries to employ token stealing to escalate their security context from the administrator level to the SYSTEM level. Once this elevation occurs, the adversary can authenticate to a remote system using the account associated with the token, provided that the account has the necessary permissions on the remote system. (Citation: Pentestlab Token Manipulation) Any standard user is able to employ the runas command, along with Windows API functions, to generate impersonation tokens without needing access to an administrator account. Additionally, other methods, such as modifications to Active Directory fields, can also be utilized to alter access tokens.

Payloads might be compressed, archived, or encrypted to evade detection. These payloads could be utilized during Initial Access or in subsequent stages to reduce the likelihood of discovery. Attack description

An adversary exploits a weakness in the way an application searches for external libraries to manipulate the execution flow to point to an adversary supplied library or code base. This pattern of attack allows the adversary to compromise the application or server via the execution of unauthorized code. An application typically makes calls to functions that are a part of libraries external to the application. These libraries may be part of the operating system or they may be third party libraries. If an adversary can redirect an application's attempts to access these libraries to other libraries that the adversary supplies, the adversary will be able to force the targeted application to execute arbitrary code. This is especially dangerous if the targeted application has enhanced privileges. Access can be redirected through a number of techniques, including the use of symbolic links, search path modification, and relative path manipulation.

Prerequisites

- The attacker must have knowledge of a specific username to aim for.
- The system employs password-based authentication as its sole authentication factor.
- The application lacks a password throttling mechanism. An effective password throttling mechanism would render brute forcing a password nearly impossible from a computational standpoint, either by locking the user out after a predetermined number of failed attempts or by implementing timeout intervals. Both of these strategies would render a brute force attack impractical.

ATT&CK adversary context

**Technique:** Brute Force

Adversaries can employ brute force methods to access accounts when they do not know the passwords or when they have obtained password hashes. (Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) In situations where an adversary lacks the password for one or more accounts, they may methodically guess the password by utilizing a repetitive or iterative approach. (Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) The process of brute forcing passwords can occur through interactions with a service that verifies the validity of those credentials or performed offline against previously obtained credential data, such as password hashes.

Credential brute forcing can occur at different stages during a breach. For instance, adversaries might try to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a target environment, leveraging information gathered from other post-compromise activities like [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Additionally, adversaries may integrate brute forcing efforts with activities such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of their Initial Access strategy.

If an adversary correctly guesses a password but is unable to log into a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they might modify their infrastructure until it aligns with the victim's location, thus circumventing those policies. (Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)

ATT&CK adversary context **Technique:** Thread Execution Hijacking Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Thread Execution Hijacking is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Thread Execution Hijacking is commonly performed by suspending an existing process then unmapping/hollowing its memory, which can then be replaced with malicious code or the path to a DLL. A handle to an existing victim process is first created with native Windows API calls such as OpenThread. At this point the process can be suspended then written to, realigned to the injected code, and resumed via SuspendThread , VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, then ResumeThread respectively.(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) This is very similar to [Process Hollowing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012) but targets an existing process rather than creating a process in a suspended state. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via Thread Execution Hijacking may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
